described: Tall herb of wet alpine meadow and stream side. Huge kidney-shaped basal leaves as wide as a plate on long stalks, then a tall torch of bright yellow daisy heads whose ray florets are long narrow straps. Root boiled for cough. First thing seen: round leaves at the ground, yellow torch above.
traits: strap ray floret; huge round basal leaf; yellow spike; wet alpine meadow; cough root
name: tongue + flower
why: The Latin ligula is a little tongue and names the strap ray, which is the one trait true of every species and visible on meeting it.

described: Legume shrub or herb with pinnate leaves, spikes of small pink-purple pea flowers and slender pods. The leaves ferment to a deep blue, and this is the plant that dyed the world's cloth blue for three thousand years.
traits: blue dye from leaves; pea flower; pinnate leaf; shrub
name: blue + dye
why: Latin indigo-bearing and Chinese wood blue say the same thing. The plant is not blue, it MAKES blue, so dye carries the sense that colour alone would lose.

described: Leafy liverwort of wet shaded forest, growing on bark and rock in flat overlapping feathery mats, translucent green, each shoot a double row of round toothed leaves like a feather laid flat.
traits: feather-flat shoot; overlapping leaves; wet shade; bark and rock; translucent green
name: feather + moss
why: The Chinese calls it feather moss and that is exactly what the mats look like. Minimal, and a person meeting it would guess it.

described: Shrub with opposite pleated strongly veined leaves, a flat white plate of flowers often ringed with larger sterile ones, then clusters of red or black berries. Straight young shoots were cut for arrow shafts, which is where the English name comes from.
traits: flat white flower plate; red berry; opposite pleated leaf; straight shoots for arrows
name: arrow + wood
why: Flat white cyme and red drupe are shared with too many shrubs. The straight arrow shoot is a use, is what English already calls it, and is what matters to someone who needs a shaft.

described: Alpine thistle of high stony ground, wrapped in dense white wool, the snow lotus swaddled in translucent woolly bracts that trap the sun's heat at altitude. Purple thistle heads buried in the wool.
traits: dense white wool; alpine and high stony; thistle head; bracts trapping heat
name: wool + thistle
why: Chinese wind-hair points at the same wool. Wool separates it from every other thistle, and it is the first thing a hand feels.

described: Square-stemmed herb with opposite leaves and small dull maroon-brown pitcher flowers that wasps work. Rank smell when bruised. The dark tuberous root is dug for fever and swelling.
traits: square stem; small brown helmet flower; rank smell; dark medicinal tuber
name: dark + root
why: Chinese xuan shen is dark root, and the root is the whole reason the plant is known and gathered. The flowers are too dull to name it by.

described: Fleshy translucent jointed stem, and a leaf that is plainly LOPSIDED, one half larger than the other, often silver-marked or red beneath. Pink or white flowers, winged triangular seed cases. The stem is sharply sour and is eaten as a sour vegetable.
traits: lopsided asymmetric leaf; fleshy jointed stem; sour juice; winged seed case
name: crooked + leaf
why: The unequal leaf is unique in the whole flora and is the first thing anyone notices. Nothing else needs saying.

described: Stout prickly stem carrying the largest compound leaves in the temperate wood, with a frothy head of tiny white flowers and black berries. The young spring shoot is cut and eaten before the prickles harden.
traits: thick prickly stem; enormous compound leaf; edible spring shoot; white froth of flowers
name: thorn + shoot
why: Chinese song mu is thorn tree. Thorn alone fits too many shrubs, so the edible shoot is added, which is also why people go to it.

described: An orchid with no leaves and no green at all, living on the fungus in the forest floor. A bare brown or straw stalk pushes up carrying dull tubular flowers, then dies back. The underground tuber is dug for headache and dizziness.
traits: no leaves, no green; bare stalk; feeds on fungus; tuber for headache
name: bare + orchid
why: Leaflessness is total and is the first thing seen, a stalk standing with nothing on it. No other orchid here is bare.

described: Tufted perennial grass of damp meadow and hillside, with a fine feathery flower head and a tuft of long hairs at the base of each floret, standing shorter than a true reed.
traits: tufted; feathery panicle; hairs at floret base; damp meadow; reed-like but small
name: small + reed
why: English already calls the group small-reed. Two parts, true of the genus, and it places the plant beside the reed it resembles.

described: Spiny shrub carrying three-pronged thorns at each node and rosettes of small spoon-shaped leaves. Hanging yellow flowers, then oblong scarlet berries sharp enough to make the mouth water. Cut the stem and the wood and inner bark are BRIGHT YELLOW, and that yellow is both dye and medicine.
traits: three-pronged thorn; bright yellow inner wood; red sour berry; yellow hanging flower
name: yellow + thorn
why: Thorn and berry alone would take in rose and bramble. The yellow wood under the bark is unique, valuable, and paired with the thorn names it exactly.

described: Herb of high short turf, often with deep blue trumpet flowers that open to the sun and shut in cloud. The root is ferociously bitter, the standard bitter tonic east and west, dug for the liver.
traits: deep blue trumpet; alpine turf; violently bitter root; opens to sun
name: bitter + root
why: Chinese long dan is dragon's bile, the same bitterness. Not every species is blue but every one is bitter, so bitterness is the accurate half.

described: A flat rosette of thick wrinkled hairy leaves pressed against wet shaded limestone cliff in the south-west, throwing up slender stalks of nodding bell flowers in yellow, orange or purple.
traits: rosette flat on wet cliff; thick wrinkled hairy leaf; nodding bell flower; limestone shade
name: cliff + bell
why: The Latin mountain-grace is vague. Where it lives and what the flower is shaped like are both exact and both visible at a glance.

described: Tropical legume tree and liana with pinnate leaves, small white pea flowers and flat papery pods. The heartwood is dense, dark red-brown and FRAGRANT, and it is the rosewood of furniture and instruments, the most trafficked timber on earth.
traits: fragrant dense heartwood; dark red-brown wood; pea flower; papery pod; prized timber
name: scent + wood
why: Red wood alone fits many timbers. The fragrance of the heartwood is what separates rosewood from all of them and is why it is cut.

described: Tufted grass of dry steppe. Every seed carries a long twisted awn, feathered or needle-fine, that turns with the damp and drills the sharp seed into the soil, and into the wool and skin of whatever walks through.
traits: long twisted awn; needle-sharp seed that drills; dry steppe; feathery plume
name: needle + grass
why: The Chinese says needle grass and the seed really does work like a needle. Minimal, exact, and anyone who has walked through it knows.

described: Tall herb or shrub with nettle-like toothed opposite leaves, often white-felted beneath, but WITHOUT the sting. The bast under the bark strips into ramie, among the strongest fibres there is, spun for cloth and laid into rope.
traits: nettle leaf without sting; white felt beneath; very strong bast fibre; cloth and rope
name: rope + nettle
why: It looks like a nettle and is used like flax. Naming it by the fibre says why anyone walks to it, and nettle places the leaf.

described: Soft finely cut fern of damp wood, fronds twice or three times divided into lace, rising in a shuttlecock crown from a brittle pale or reddish stalk. Under the frond the spore covers curve like a hoof.
traits: lacy twice-cut frond; shuttlecock crown; brittle pale stalk; hoof-curved spore cover; damp wood
name: hoof + fern
why: Lacy fits half the ferns there are. The hooked spore cover is diagnostic, and the Chinese had already picked it out as the hoof.

described: Tufted grass of cold high plateau sand and gravel, with a dense bristly spike in the wheat tribe, grazed hard by yak where almost nothing else grows.
traits: wheat-like bristly spike; cold high plateau; sand and gravel; grazed by yak
name: high + wheat + grass
why: No feature of the plant itself is distinctive, so the name is where it grows and what it belongs to. It grows higher than any of its relatives.

described: Small tree whose whole underside is covered in woolly star-shaped hairs, often with rust-red or golden glands. Broad, often three-lobed leaves. The fruit of one species is rubbed for kamala, a brilliant red-orange dye powder.
traits: woolly star hairs all over; rust-red glands; broad three-lobed leaf; red dye from fruit
name: wool + tree
why: The Latin means fleecy and the wool is on every species. The red dye belongs to one species only, so it cannot carry the genus.

described: Herb with opposite leaves and a five-petalled notched white or pink flower sitting in an INFLATED BLADDER of a calyx. The stems of many are glandular and sticky enough to hold a fly, and some open and give scent only at dusk for moths.
traits: inflated bladder calyx; sticky stem that traps flies; notched petal; night scent
name: sticky + flower
why: Latin names it for foam-covered Silenus and Chinese calls it fly grass. Both point at the stickiness, so two independent witnesses agree.

described: Tall herb with deeply cut dark palmate leaves and deep blue-purple flowers whose upper sepal arches into a HELMET. The tuberous root is among the deadliest things that grow, smeared on arrow and spear, and given in minute processed doses for pain.
traits: helmet-hooded flower; deep blue-purple; deadly tuber; arrow poison; cut palmate leaf
name: hood + flower
why: The hood is unmistakable, unique among blue flowers, and is what is seen first. The poison is famous but invisible.

described: Clumping bamboo of the warm south, hollow jointed woody stems rising in a dense tuft, with sharp thorny branches tangled about the base of the clump.
traits: clumping not running; thorny branches at the base; hollow jointed stem; warm south
name: thorn + bamboo
why: Chinese le zhu is thorn bamboo exactly. The thorns at the clump base separate it from every other bamboo here.

described: Thorny scrambling shrub with small glossy opposite leaves, spikes of tiny fragrant flowers and small purple-black sweet-sour fruits that birds strip. Leaves are brewed as tea, and the twisted stems are trained as bonsai.
traits: thorny scrambler; tiny plum-like fruit; birds strip it; glossy small leaf; leaf tea
name: bird + plum
why: The Chinese sparrow plum vine names the fruit and the birds together, which is how anyone meets the plant, following a flock into the thicket.

described: Legume shrub whose flowers hide inside conspicuous folded leafy bracts like a closed fan. The deep taproot is so firmly set that the Chinese name says it would take a thousand pounds to pull it out, and that root is what is dug for medicine.
traits: folded fan-like bracts; hidden flower; immovably deep taproot; trifoliate leaf
name: strong + root
why: The Chinese name is entirely about the root that will not come out, and the root is what is gathered. Nothing above ground is as telling.

described: Dwarf bamboo carrying very large broad leaves, low in the forest understorey. The leaf is the point: it wraps rice dumplings, is sewn into rain hats, and is laid over boat awnings.
traits: very broad large leaf; dwarf bamboo; leaf wraps food; leaf for rain hats
name: wrap + bamboo
why: The Chinese character ruo names the broad bamboo leaf used for wrapping. The use is the identity, and it is short.

described: Huge tropical liana with trifoliate leaves, throwing down long ropes hung with chains of dark claw-shaped flowers. The pods are covered in orange hairs that break off in the skin and itch savagely for days. Big glossy sea beans drift oceans and wash up whole.
traits: stinging itch hairs on the pod; giant climbing rope; claw flowers in hanging chains; drifting glossy bean
name: itch + vine
why: Everyone who has touched the pod remembers only the itch. It is unique, it is the first thing learned about the plant, and it is two words.

described: Small soft grass of marsh edge and wet ditch with lance-shaped leaves and an open airy head of tiny round paired grains, the two of a pair alike in size and ripening together.
traits: paired equal grains; open airy head; wet ground; small round spikelet
name: twin + grain
why: The Latin says equal chaff and means the paired florets, which is the one character that holds across the genus and can be seen in the hand.

described: Bulb in the ground, hollow or strap leaves, a globe of star flowers on a bare stalk. Crush any part of it and the smell is unmistakable and sharp enough to sting the eyes. Onion, garlic, leek and chive are all this one kind.
traits: bulb; pungent sulphur smell; globe umbel; hollow leaf; the oldest kitchen plant
name: onion
why: The whole genus is the onion kind and every language already has one word for it. Adding a describing word would be adding one nobody needs.

described: Fern of damp forest floor with broad once or twice cut fronds rising from a stout crown, the spore lines set in pairs back to back along each vein. The coiled young fronds are picked and eaten across Asia.
traits: paired back-to-back spore lines; broad cut frond; edible fiddlehead; damp forest
name: twin + fern
why: Chinese and Latin agree on the doubling, and the paired spore lines separate it from every fern beside it.

described: Giant herb whose trunk is nothing but rolled leaf bases. Enormous paddle leaves tear along their veins in wind into a ragged fan. A heavy purple bud hangs down and opens hand after hand of fruit.
traits: false trunk of rolled leaves; huge paddle leaf shredding in wind; hanging purple bud; hands of fruit
name: banana
why: The fruit is among the most eaten things on earth and already has a single word everywhere. A compound here would be longer and say less.

described: Low crucifer rooted in cold running mountain water, heart-shaped leaves on long stalks, small white cross flowers. The thick green rhizome grated fresh is fiercely pungent, and the heat runs up into the nose rather than burning the tongue.
traits: cold running water; heart leaf; green rhizome; heat that goes up the nose
name: nose + fire
why: The burn is unlike any other pungency because of where it is felt, and that is exactly what the two words say. Anyone who has eaten it knows the name at once.

described: Grass-like plant of wood and moor with flat soft leaves fringed all along their edges with long white hairs that hold dew and catch the light. Clusters of small brown papery flowers.
traits: long white hairs fringing the leaf edge; dew caught on the hairs; flat grassy leaf; brown papery flower
name: hair + rush
why: The fringe of hairs is the one character that tells it from every true rush at a glance, and it is why the Latin name means glowworm.

described: Thick dark lance-shaped leaves standing straight out of deep shade, enduring drought, dark and neglect for years. The flowers are the strange part: fleshy purple-brown cups sitting ON THE GROUND among the leaf bases, worked by gnats and springtails.
traits: flowers at ground level among the leaf bases; tough dark leathery leaf; deep shade; almost unkillable
name: ground + flower
why: A flower opening on the soil itself is rare enough to name by, and once seen it is never mistaken. Toughness is shared with too many plants.

described: Tree of the mallow kin with leathery simple leaves and showy fragrant heads of white or pink flowers, each one pushing out a long slender column far beyond the petals with the anthers crowded at its tip. Woody pear-shaped capsules split to loose winged seeds.
traits: long protruding stamen column; fragrant white or pink head; winged seed from a woody capsule; bark fibre
name: pillar + flower
why: The column standing out of the flower is unmistakable and is the character the genus is built on.

described: A perfect steel-blue SPHERE of spiny flowers held on a stout stem above deeply cut prickly leaves that are grey and woolly beneath. Bees work the globe all around.
traits: ball of blue spiny flowers; prickly cut leaf; grey wool beneath; stout stem
name: thorn + ball
why: The Latin says hedgehog face and the Chinese says blue thorn head. Both point at the same spiny sphere, and no other plant makes one.

described: Shrub of the rose kin with arching canes and doubly toothed lobed leaves, hung with slender drooping strings of small tubular pink or white flowers, one after another like beads on a thread.
traits: drooping thread of small tubular flowers; arching cane; lobed doubly toothed leaf; small dry inflated fruit
name: thread + flower
why: Chinese calls it the embroidery-thread plum for that thin hanging string of flowers, which is exactly what is seen first.

described: One or two leaves split into a spread of fingers, and beside them a striped HOOD arching over a standing spike, often drawn out into a long whip. Raw, it burns the mouth raw with needle crystals. In autumn the spike becomes a scarlet cob of berries.
traits: striped hood over a standing spike; fingered leaf; whip-like tail; burns the mouth; scarlet berry cob
name: snake + hood
why: The hood is striped and arched exactly like a cobra raised to strike, which is what its English name says too, and the hood alone is already taken by the monkshood.

described: Orchid creeping along bark or rock, its rhizome set at intervals with rounded swollen bulbs, each carrying one thick leaf. The flowers are often hinged and rock in the least air, and many smell of carrion to bring flies.
traits: swollen round bulb at intervals; one thick leaf per bulb; creeping on bark and rock; hinged rocking flower; carrion smell
name: bulb + leaf
why: The Latin says bulb leaf and the Chinese says stone bean, the same swollen bulb seen twice. It is the character that makes the genus recognisable.

described: Small herb of damp shade with watery TRANSLUCENT stems that snap wetly, opposite leaves often banded with silver, and tiny green flowers that fire their pollen in a small visible puff when they ripen.
traits: translucent watery stem; silver-banded leaf; damp shade; pollen fired in a puff
name: clear + stem
why: The stem is see-through, which almost nothing else here is, and it is the first thing noticed on picking one.

described: Flat plate of tiny white or pink daisies on a stiff stem above leaves cut so finely they look like feathers. Sharp aromatic smell when crushed. Pressed on a cut it slows the bleeding, and it has been the wound herb of every people that has met it.
traits: feather-fine cut leaf; flat white plate of flowers; sharp aromatic smell; staunches bleeding
name: wound + herb
why: Every people that met it named it for staunching blood: staunchweed, soldier's woundwort, nosebleed plant. The use is older and steadier than any look.

described: A cone-bearing plant wearing the clothes of a flowering one: woody liana with swollen jointed nodes and opposite glossy leathery oval leaves exactly like a broadleaf tree's, but the seeds sit naked in fleshy red coats along a spike. The bark strips into strong cord for nets, and the seeds are pounded into crackers.
traits: liana with jointed swollen nodes; broadleaf-looking leaves on a cone plant; naked red seed on a spike; strong bark cordage
name: rope + vine
why: The bark cord is why anyone climbs to it, and liana places it. Chinese names it the hemp vine for the same fibre.

described: Short grass with a dense spike-like head that turns from green to yellow-brown. It is the grass that makes hay smell of hay: dry a handful and the scent of new-mown meadow and vanilla comes off it for months.
traits: the smell of drying hay; dense yellow-brown spike; short grass; meadow
name: sweet + grass
why: The scent is the entire reason the plant is known, is unmistakable, and is already its name in English. Nothing about the look would separate it.

described: Low herb or small shrub whose leaves split into five toothed fingers from a single point, under flat five-petalled flowers, almost always bright yellow, ringed with an extra outer collar of bracts. The silvery-leaved one has roots that were dug in hunger years.
traits: five fingers from one point; flat five-petalled yellow flower; outer ring of bracts; famine root
name: five + leaf
why: The five leaflets are the genus in one word and are what the English cinquefoil already says. They are countable on meeting the plant.

described: Tall herb with ragged deeply cut leaves and a dense flat head of hard bright yellow daisies. It poisons the liver of horses and cattle slowly and they die months after eating it, so it is grubbed out of every pasture. Black and orange caterpillars strip it bare.
traits: flat head of hard yellow daisies; ragged cut leaf; slow liver poison to stock; black and orange caterpillar
name: poison + daisy
why: Yellow daisies are everywhere and the poison is what sets this one apart. It is also the thing anyone keeping animals most needs the name to say.

described: Herb with pinnately cut leaves under a broad flat spray of tiny yellow or white flowers. The whole plant, and the root worst of all, stinks of soured bean sauce and old cloth, and the smell carries on the hand long after.
traits: stink of soured sauce; flat spray of small yellow flowers; cut leaf; root used for abscess
name: rot + smell
why: The Chinese name is simply spoiled sauce. The smell reaches a person before the plant is even found, and nothing else about it is distinctive.

described: Orchid with long strap leaves rising in a fan from a squat bulb, sending up arching sprays of waxy flowers that last for months, green and brown and yellow, with a boat-shaped lip. The scent is faint and clean, and it has stood for the scholar and the gentleman in painting and verse for two thousand years.
traits: boat-shaped lip; strap leaves in a fan; long-lasting waxy flower; faint clean scent
name: boat + orchid
why: The Latin names the boat of the lip. Chinese gives this genus the bare word orchid, so the added word has to be small and true, and the lip is both.

described: Running bamboo of high cold mountain forest, slender canes spreading on long underground necks into dense thickets under the trees. Pandas live on it.
traits: high cold mountain forest; running underground necks; dense understorey thicket; slender cane; panda food
name: high + bamboo
why: Altitude is what separates it from every other bamboo here, and the other bamboos are already named by thorn and by wrapping leaf.

described: Evergreen with thick glossy dark leathery leaves and bold waxy flowers, white or pink or red, around a boss of yellow stamens. Hard round woody capsules hold big oily seeds pressed for cooking oil. The dried young leaves of one of them are all the tea in the world.
traits: thick glossy leathery leaf; waxy flower with a yellow stamen boss; oily seed; the tea leaf
name: tea + flower
why: Chinese calls it mountain tea. Tea names what the genus gave the world and flower keeps it apart from the drink itself.

described: Fern riding on bark or bare rock, its creeping scaly rhizome pressed flat to the surface, throwing up thick leathery fronds, sometimes simple straps, sometimes lobed, with spore patches sunk into pits on the underside.
traits: thick leathery frond; creeping on bark and rock; sunken spore pits; simple or lobed strap
name: leather + fern
why: The frond is stiff and leathery to the hand, unlike the lacy ferns of the ground, which is what its rock and bark life demands.

described: Tall soft grass standing in shallow water and ditch, broad bright green leaves floating and bending on the surface, with a wide spreading head of long narrow spikelets. The grain is sweet and was gathered and boiled as groats.
traits: sweet grain gathered as food; standing in shallow water; broad soft floating leaf; long narrow spikelet
name: sweet + grain
why: Latin and Chinese both say sweet. The grain is the part that is sweet and the part that was eaten, and sweet grass is already taken by the hay grass.

described: Tiny leafy liverwort making flat dark mats, reddish brown to almost black-purple, pressed to tree bark and rock. Under a lens each leaf carries a small hollow pitcher folded beneath it, shaped like an ear, which holds water through a drought and sometimes a rotifer with it. Loggers who handle the bark come out in a rash.
traits: ear-shaped water pouch under each leaf; dark red-brown to purple mats; flat on bark and rock; causes a rash on handling
name: ear + moss
why: The Chinese names it ear-leaf for that folded pouch, which is the one character that separates it from every other liverwort, and feather is already taken by Plagiochila.

described: Yellow daisy heads, often with few rays or none, over ragged leaves. When the seed sets, the head turns into a ball of pure white hair and then goes bald, which is why the Latin calls it the old man.
traits: white-haired seed head going bald; yellow daisy head; few or no rays; ragged leaf
name: white + head
why: The Latin is senex, an old man, and means the white seed head. It is what the plant looks like for most of the season and it tells it from the other yellow daisies.

described: Sedge of wet open ground, with dense brown spikelets held in a loose umbel on slender stems that sway in any wind. The style is fringed with fine hairs along its edge and drops away once the seed is set.
traits: fringed style; brown spikelet in an umbel; wet open ground; swaying slender stem
name: fringe + sedge
why: The fringe on the style is what the Latin names and is the character that holds across the genus. Swaying, which the Chinese picked, is true of half the wet-ground plants there are.

described: Herb or low shrub with opposite leaves and tubular flowers split into two clear lips, white, pink or red, crowded into bracted spikes. The ripe capsule dries, splits with a snap and throws its seeds off small hooks.
traits: two-lipped tubular flower; bracted spike; capsule that snaps open and throws seed; opposite leaf
name: lip + flower
why: The two-lipped flower is on every species and is what is seen. The exploding capsule is shared with the whole family around it, so it cannot tell this one apart.

described: Low creeper of damp ground running on red runners, with pinnate leaves that are silky SILVER-WHITE underneath and flash when the wind turns them. Single yellow five-petalled flowers. The roots were dug in hunger years and taste of parsnip and chestnut.
traits: silver-white silky leaf underside; creeping red runners; yellow five-petal flower; famine root
name: silver + leaf
why: The Latin is silver and the underside really does flash white across a whole meadow when the wind turns. Five leaves is already Potentilla, which this was split from.

described: Evergreen with thick glossy leaves, often armed with hard spines along the edge, small dull white flowers, and brilliant red berries that hold on the bare winter branches until the birds strip them. Poisonous to people. The wood is white and very hard.
traits: evergreen through winter; glossy spined leaf; red berry held all winter; hard white wood
name: winter + green
why: The Chinese dong qing is winter green, and staying green and berried through the dead of the year is the whole reason anyone notices the tree.

described: Tall coarse blue-grey grass of sand dune and salt steppe, with thick cords of rhizome running through loose sand and binding it. A dense stiff spike like a head of wheat stands above.
traits: blue-grey coarse leaf; binds loose sand with thick rhizome; dune and salt steppe; stiff wheat-like spike
name: sand + rye
why: It is the wild rye of sand, which places the plant and says where it grows in two words. Holding the dune together is also the only reason it is ever planted.

described: Climbing gourd vine with tendrils and palmate leaves of five to nine leaflets, carrying small greenish flowers. Under the ground sits a heavy pale tuber that is violently bitter, dug and dried for dysentery and inflammation.
traits: large violently bitter tuber; tendril climber; palmate leaflets; small green flower
name: bitter + vine
why: Chinese xue dan is snow gall, pale and bitter, and the bitterness is why it is dug. Bitter root already belongs to the gentian, so the climbing habit does the separating.

described: A huge umbellifer. Thick hollow ridged stems, deeply lobed leaves as long as an arm, and a flat white flower plate the size of a dinner plate. The sap on skin in sunlight raises burns and blisters that scar and come back for years.
traits: enormous size; thick hollow ridged stem; broad flat white umbel; sap that blisters skin in sunlight
name: blister + weed
why: The size is what is seen and the sap is what matters. Anyone cutting a path through it needs the name to carry the warning, and no other umbellifer here burns.

described: Low soft herb with grey-green opposite leaves covered in fine hair, each the size and shape of a mouse's ear. Small white flowers whose five petals are split so deeply they look like ten. The seed case is a small curved horn.
traits: soft grey hairy leaf like a mouse ear; deeply split white petal; curved horn seed case; low mat
name: mouse + ear
why: English, Chinese and the hand all agree: the leaf is a mouse's ear, in size, shape and softness. Three independent witnesses on one trait is as good as it gets.

described: Woody climbing legume of the tropics with pinnate leaves and sprays of pink-white pea flowers. The root, pounded and stirred into a pool, brings the fish up stunned to the surface within minutes, and it is used the same way against insects on a crop.
traits: root that stuns fish in water; woody tropical liana; pinnate leaf; pea flower
name: fish + poison
why: Chinese yu teng is fish vine. Stunning fish with a pounded root is old technology practised on three continents, and it is the entire reason this plant is known.

described: Shrub throwing long arching canes, with lance leaves white-felted beneath and long tapering cones of small honey-scented purple flowers. On a warm day the cones are covered in butterflies, several to a spike.
traits: long tapering flower cone; honey scent; covered in butterflies; arching cane; white-felted leaf
name: butterfly + bush
why: This is already its name in English and the reason is visible from across a field. Chinese calls it drunk-fish grass for a second use, but the butterflies are what anyone meets first.

described: Evergreen tree of the tea kin with thick leathery leaves, silky brown hairs lying flat on the underside and along the young shoots. Single nodding white flowers hang under the branch on a hooked stalk, crowded with stamens, then a dark berry.
traits: silky hairs flat on the leaf underside; thick leathery leaf; nodding white flower; crowded stamens
name: silk + leaf
why: The Latin names the crowded stamens, which needs a lens and a flower. The silky underside is there all year and is what the hand finds first.

described: Low fleshy herb of the high cold plateau, with smooth thick basal leaves shaped and held exactly like a hare's ear, and a dense short spike of blue-purple two-lipped flowers pushed up among them.
traits: leaf shaped like a hare's ear; thick fleshy basal leaf; dense blue-purple spike; high cold plateau
name: hare + ear
why: The Latin is hare's ear and the Chinese is rabbit ear grass. Two traditions that never met picked the same image, which means it is the thing anyone sees.

described: Aromatic herb or low shrub with finely cut grey-green leaves, white and woolly beneath, and small drab flower heads that need no insect. Crush a leaf and the smell is sharp, bitter and clinging. It is burned on the skin as moxa, steeped against fever, and it flavours the bitter drinks.
traits: sharp bitter clinging smell; finely cut grey leaf, white beneath; drab wind-pollinated heads; burned as moxa; bitter drink
name: bitter + leaf
why: The bitterness is in every species and in every use, burning, steeping and flavouring, and it is the leaf that carries it. Wound herb is already the yarrow.

described: Toothed opposite leaves on a square stem, and over every surface fine hollow hairs that break off in the skin and inject a burn that lasts for hours. Boiled, the young tops lose the sting and are eaten, and the stem strips into strong cord.
traits: stinging hairs that burn for hours; toothed opposite leaf; young tops eaten once boiled; strong stem fibre
name: nettle
why: This is the nettle itself, the plant the word means. Every other nettle-like thing here is named by reference to it, so it cannot be named by reference to them.

described: Mint-family herb with a square stem, wrinkled hairy opposite leaves, and two-lipped yellow or purple flowers set in tight WHORLS that ring the stem at intervals like beads on a rod. Root tubers are dug and eaten.
traits: flowers in rings around the stem; square stem; wrinkled hairy leaf; edible root tuber
name: ring + flower
why: The flowers stand in complete rings up the stem, spaced like rungs, which is unmistakable at a glance and unlike the spikes and heads around it.

described: Clumping bamboo of high mountain forest, its canes slender, straight and stiff, standing in dense thickets under the trees. The canes are cut for arrow shafts. Pandas live in it and on it.
traits: slender straight stiff cane; arrow shafts; dense high-forest thicket; clumping; panda food
name: arrow + bamboo
why: Chinese jian zhu is arrow bamboo. A straight stiff shaft of the right thickness is a use worth naming by, and it separates this from the thorn and wrapping bamboos.

described: Small sprawling herb with a single line of hairs running down one side of the stem, and small white flowers whose five petals are split so deeply to the base that the flower reads as a ten-rayed star. Eaten as a pot-herb and thrown to the hens.
traits: five petals split to look like ten rays; star-shaped white flower; one line of hairs down the stem; eaten as greens
name: star + flower
why: Latin stella and English starwort both say star, and the split petals really do make one. The line of hairs is the surer character but needs a lens.

described: Round smooth green stems standing in wet ground with no leaf to speak of, holding a small brown cluster of flowers out of one side. Split a stem and the white spongy pith pulls out in one piece: soaked in fat it burns as a rushlight, and the stems are woven into mats.
traits: round smooth leafless green stem; white pith drawn out for a wick; wet ground; woven into mats
name: rush
why: This is the rush itself. The woodrush beside it is named hair rush by reference to this, so naming this one by reference to anything would leave the pair with no anchor.

described: Leafless green cylindrical stems standing close in wet mud, each one topped by a single small brown spikelet like the head of a match. One of them swells a sweet crisp white corm under the mud that is dug, peeled and eaten raw.
traits: one spikelet at the tip like a match head; leafless round stem; wet mud; sweet crisp corm
name: spike + rush
why: A single terminal spikelet on a leafless stem is the whole genus in one look, and spike rush is already what English calls it.

described: Whole plant clothed in long silver silky hair. Large nodding bell flowers, purple or white, open low on the bare ground in early spring before the leaves are properly out, then the seed heads draw out into long feathered plumes that catch the wind.
traits: long silver silky hair everywhere; nodding bell flower; opens before the leaves in early spring; feathered plume seeds
name: silk + bell
why: The silky coat and the hanging bell are both there the moment the plant appears, and together nothing else is like it. White head is already the groundsel.

described: Evergreen shrub low in the forest shade, with thick glossy leaves whose scalloped edges are dotted with dark glands, small starry white or pink flowers, and round bright red berries that hang near the ground and last most of a year.
traits: round bright red berry lasting most of a year; glossy leaf with dark gland dots; deep forest shade; low shrub
name: red + bead
why: The berries are round, hard, glossy and hang in strings near the ground for months, so they read as beads and they are what is seen in the shade all winter.

described: Flat rosette of leaves cut into backward-pointing teeth, a hollow stalk that bleeds white milk when broken, one solid golden head packed with rays, and then a perfect grey sphere of parachute seeds that goes on one breath. Leaves eaten, root roasted.
traits: backward-pointing leaf teeth; white milky sap; solid golden head; perfect sphere of parachute seeds
name: tooth + leaf
why: A dozen languages name it the lion's tooth from those leaf teeth, and they are on the plant all year, while the golden head and the seed sphere are each there for a week.

described: Orchid living on a tree, its cane-like jointed stems hanging in bunches from the bark with no soil at all, carrying showy flowers along their length. The canes of some are dried and chewed or simmered for thirst and a weak stomach.
traits: lives on tree bark with no soil; cane-like jointed stems hanging; showy flowers along the cane; canes simmered as a tonic
name: tree + orchid
why: The Latin says life on a tree and that is the fact about it: an orchid rooted on bark rather than in ground. Stone orchid, the Chinese, names the minority that sit on rock.

described: Thorny tree with zigzag twigs, each node armed with a pair of spines, one straight and one hooked back. Glossy three-veined leaves, small yellow-green flowers, and a sweet crisp fruit that dries to a wrinkled red date and keeps for years.
traits: paired spines, one straight one hooked; zigzag twig; three-veined glossy leaf; sweet fruit dried as a red date
name: thorn + date
why: The dried fruit is the reason it is grown and is called a date across Asia, and the paired hook-and-straight spines keep it apart from the palm that word otherwise names.

described: Fast tall tree of riverbank and floodplain. The leaf stalk is flattened sideways, so the least air sets every leaf turning and the whole crown hisses when nothing else moves. Catkins first, then drifts of white cotton carrying the seed. Soft pale wood.
traits: flattened leaf stalk that makes the leaves tremble; crown that hisses in the least wind; white cotton seed drifts; riverbank; soft pale wood
name: tremble + leaf
why: No other tree moves like it and the sound carries further than the sight. It is one mechanical fact, the flattened stalk, and it is what the tree is known for everywhere it grows.

described: Tree with lopsided toothed leaves on three main veins, and grey bark broken into corky warts and ridges that get rougher with age. Small sweet drupes with a crunchy stone that the birds take through winter.
traits: grey bark in corky warts and ridges; lopsided three-veined leaf; small sweet stone fruit; birds strip it
name: wart + bark
why: The warty corky bark is there in every season and on every age of tree, and it is what the hand finds. The leaf is lopsided but so is the elm beside it.

described: Reed-like leafy stems from a knobbly branching rhizome that lies just under the soil. Cut it and the smell is sharp and warm and the taste burns the back of the mouth. It is dug green or dried and ground, and there is hardly a kitchen without it.
traits: knobbly branching rhizome; sharp warm pungent burn; reed-like leafy stem; in every kitchen
name: hot + root
why: The heat of the root is the whole point of the plant and is what every use turns on. It sits beside the other named roots, bitter, dark and strong, and is told apart from all of them.

described: Succulent of high cold rock and arctic ledge, with fleshy blue-green leaves crowded on short stems rising from a thick woody rootstock. Cut that rootstock and it smells clearly of roses. Dug and dried against cold, altitude and exhaustion.
traits: root that smells of roses when cut; fleshy blue-green succulent leaf; high cold rock ledge; taken against exhaustion
name: rose + root
why: The Latin says rose and the smell is real, unexpected and unmistakable on a bare mountain. It is also exactly the part that is dug, so the name says what is gathered.

described: Legume vine that grows a hand's width in a day and buries a hillside, shrub and tree under one unbroken sheet of trifoliate leaves. Purple pea flowers that smell of grapes. Under it all a tuber the size of a man, dug and washed for a fine white starch, and the stem stripped for cloth fibre.
traits: enormous starchy tuber washed for white flour; grows fast enough to bury a hillside; trifoliate leaf; grape-scented purple flower
name: flour + vine
why: The washed starch is what the plant is grown and dug for, and vine says how it gets there. Smothering is the more striking sight but it is a habit of a dozen climbers.

described: Ginger-family, tall leafy canes standing in forest shade, with showy white and red flowers carrying one large flared lip, and a red or orange capsule. The rhizome is aromatic and sharp and is used as a spice where ginger is not grown.
traits: aromatic sharp rhizome; tall leafy cane; large flared flower lip; red capsule; forest shade
name: wild + ginger
why: Chinese shan jiang is mountain ginger: the same hot root growing untended on a hillside rather than in a bed. Wild carries that, and the root does the rest.

described: Tall leafy canes from a shallow rhizome, topped by a spike of large flowers, mostly pure white, some orange, that open towards dusk. The scent is heavy and sweet and fills a whole garden after dark, and the flower spike looks like snow caught on the stem.
traits: large pure white flower opening at dusk; heavy sweet night scent; spike like caught snow; tall leafy cane
name: sweet + snow
why: The Latin is hedys and chion, sweet snow, and both halves are literally true: the scent and the white spike. Nothing needs adding and nothing can be taken away.

described: Spiny legume shrub of dry steppe and desert edge, with small paired leaflets whose midrib hardens and stays on as a spine when the leaflets drop. Bright yellow pea flowers, then slender pods that twist and crack open in the heat. Planted in rows to hold back the sand.
traits: leaf midrib hardening into a spine; small paired leaflets; bright yellow pea flower; pods that twist and snap; dry steppe
name: thorn + pea
why: A pea flower on a thorn bush is the whole plant, and the thorn is the leaf itself left behind, which is the character the genus is built on.

described: Laurel-family tree or shrub with smooth aromatic leaves. Crush a leaf or a green fruit and the smell is sharp citrus, closer to lemongrass than to any laurel. The peppery little fruits are dried as a spice and pressed for a clear scented oil.
traits: sharp lemon smell from leaf and fruit; laurel-family tree; peppery dried fruit as spice; scented oil
name: lemon + wood
why: The citrus smell out of a tree that looks nothing like a citrus is the surprise and the identity, and it is what the fruit is harvested for.

described: The largest plant genus here. Grass-like, but roll a stem between finger and thumb and it is solid and THREE-SIDED, with leaves in three ranks whose edges are saw-toothed enough to cut a hand drawn along them. Male and female spikes separate, and every seed sits sealed in its own little sac. Wet ground, everywhere on earth.
traits: solid three-sided stem; leaves in three ranks; saw edges that cut; seed sealed in a sac; wet ground
name: edge + grass
why: Sedges have edges is the first thing anyone is taught about them, the triangular stem is on every one of the 561 species, and it is felt rather than looked for.

described: Shrub to small tree of mountain thicket, leaves thick and leathery with rusty scales or felt beneath, and in spring the whole plant vanishes under trusses of wide bell flowers. The nectar is poisonous and honey made from it turns men mad.
traits: thick leathery leaf, rusty beneath; trusses of wide bell flowers covering the plant; mountain thicket; poisonous nectar
name: rose + tree
why: The Latin says rose tree and means it: a woody plant carrying flowers on the scale of a rose. The corpus read it as oleander, which is a different shrub entirely and already has the word.

described: Delicate herb with finely cut blue-grey leaves, carrying racemes of tubular flowers each drawn backwards into a long hollow SPUR. Purple, yellow or sky blue. The tuber is dug and dried against pain.
traits: long backward spur on every flower; finely cut blue-grey leaf; raceme; tuber dug for pain
name: spur + flower
why: The spur is on every flower of every species and is what the Latin was reaching for with the lark's crest. Naming it for the bird put a lark into 340 plant names.

described: Rosette of crinkled leaves lying flat on the ground, and from the middle a bare stalk holding an umbel of flat five-lobed flowers. It opens with the first warmth, often while snow still lies in the hollows.
traits: opens with the first warmth of spring; flat rosette of crinkled leaves; umbel on a bare stalk; flat five-lobed flower
name: spring + flower
why: Chinese bao chun hua is announce-spring flower. First, which the Latin reduces to, says nothing a person could use and was shared with Primulina over 536 species.

described: Rosette of thick quilted leaves pressed to shaded limestone cliff in the far south, often marked silver along the veins, throwing up slender stalks of narrow two-lipped trumpet flowers.
traits: rosette flat on shaded limestone; thick quilted leaf, often silver-veined; narrow trumpet flower; far south
name: cliff + trumpet
why: It shares the cliff with Oreocharis and differs in the flower, which is a narrow trumpet rather than a hanging bell, so the second word does the separating.

described: Shrub or small tree with finely toothed leaves, hung in summer with long slender drooping spires of small creamy white flowers, each spire like a bottle brush. The autumn leaf turns deep red and holds late.
traits: long drooping white flower spire; finely toothed leaf; deep red late autumn colour; shrub to small tree
name: white + spire
why: The corpus reads it as willow, which is Salix and has every right to the word. The drooping white spire is this plant's own and belongs to nothing else here.

described: Arching canes armed with prickles that curve BACKWARD like hooks and catch on anything passing. Compound leaves, white or pink flowers, and a fruit built of many small juicy beads packed onto one core.
traits: backward-hooked prickles that catch; arching cane; fruit of many small beads on a core; compound leaf
name: hook + berry
why: Chinese xuan gou zi is hanging hook. The hook is how the plant is met, usually by being caught on, and the berry is why anyone goes back to it.

described: Thorny shrub with twigs ending in a hard spine, small toothed leaves, dull green flowers, and clusters of black berries. The bark and berries purge violently and were taken for that, and the berries give a yellow dye.
traits: twigs ending in a spine; black berry; bark and berry purge violently; yellow dye
name: purge + berry
why: The purging is the whole reason it was ever gathered and named. Bramble belongs to Rubus, whose hooks and fruit are what that word means.

described: Herb of damp ground with opposite or whorled leaves, carrying yellow or white star flowers either scattered in the leaf joints or packed into a dense curved spike that hangs over like a string of pearls.
traits: dense curved white spike like strung pearls; yellow or white star flower; damp ground; creeping or upright
name: pearl + flower
why: Chinese zhen zhu cai is pearl vegetable, for that curved packed spike. The Latin is a king's name and reduced to town, which four unrelated genera then shared.

described: Sedge of acid bog and wet moor. In summer each head opens into a tuft of pure white cotton wool, long and soft, and a whole moor of them moves together in the wind and can be seen from a mile off.
traits: head of pure white cotton wool; acid bog and wet moor; moves as a whole field in wind; sedge
name: cotton + grass
why: This is already its name in English and the sight is unmistakable across a landscape. The corpus had it sharing the word onion with Allium, which is the onion.

described: Woody tropical climber whose young stems, leaf undersides and flower clusters are covered in rusty or yellowish hairs, with small flowers and a hairy flattened fruit. It runs up into the canopy on other trees.
traits: rusty hairs over stems, leaf backs and flowers; woody canopy climber; small flower; hairy flat fruit
name: hair + vine
why: The corpus reads it as violet, which is Viola. The hairiness is on every part of this plant and the climbing habit places it, and neither belongs to a violet.

described: Big tree with leaves split into five or seven large leaflets spreading from one point like fingers, upright candles of white or pink flowers in spring, and a thick spiny case that splits to one glossy brown nut too bitter to eat.
traits: five to seven leaflets from one point; upright candle of flowers; spiny case with a glossy brown nut
name: seven + leaf
why: Chinese qi ye shu is seven-leaf tree and the spread of leaflets is the thing seen from a distance and underfoot. Oak is Quercus and cannot be shared.

described: Tree or shrub with simple toothed leaves and five-petalled white or pink flowers that often open on bare wood before the leaves. The fruit is fleshy over one hard stone: plum, cherry, peach, apricot and almond are all this.
traits: fleshy fruit over one hard stone; five-petal flower on bare wood; simple toothed leaf; plum, cherry, peach, almond
name: stone + fruit
why: One hard stone in a soft fruit is what every species of the genus has and what no neighbour has. Apricot, which the corpus picked, is one species out of a hundred.

described: Tall forest tree with pinnate leaves and small white flowers, whose fruit holds a flattened stone marked with pits and ridges that read unmistakably as a small human face. The sour flesh is pickled and eaten.
traits: stone marked like a human face; tall forest tree; pinnate leaf; sour flesh pickled
name: face + seed
why: Chinese ren mian zi is human-face seed. Once the stone is seen the name is obvious and it is the reason the tree is known and the fruit collected.

described: Break any part and white milk runs. The fruit is the strange thing: a hollow fleshy bag with all the flowers sealed INSIDE it, entered only by one small wasp that crawls in and dies there. Some kinds drop roots from their branches that reach the ground and thicken into new trunks.
traits: white milky sap; hollow fruit with flowers sealed inside; one wasp per kind; aerial roots that become trunks
name: hollow + fruit
why: Cutting a fig open shows exactly this, a hollow filled with flowers, and no other plant fruits that way. The corpus was reading it as stone banyan tree, three roots for one idea.

described: Big riverside tree whose bark flakes away in plates to leave a mottle of cream, olive and grey like camouflage. Broad lobed leaves, and hard bristly seed balls that hang on long strings through the winter after the leaves are gone.
traits: bark flaking to a cream and olive mottle; seed balls hanging on strings all winter; broad lobed leaf; riverside
name: hang + ball
why: Chinese xuan ling mu is hanging bell tree. The balls swing on bare branches for half the year, which is when the tree is most looked at, and nothing else here does it.

described: Low creeping fern-ally making flat feathery sprays of tiny scale leaves set in four ranks, often shining blue-green in deep shade. One kind dries into a tight brown ball in drought and opens out green again within an hour of rain.
traits: flat feathery spray of tiny scale leaves; often iridescent blue-green; curls into a dry ball and reopens when wet; deep shade
name: curl + moss
why: Chinese juan bai is curled cypress, for the drying into a ball. The corpus read a place name into it and produced Sexi made little, which describes nothing.

described: The moss that builds the bog. Pale spongy heads packed together over acid ground, each plant holding many times its own weight in water and turning the water sour so little else will grow. Dead layers below it press slowly into peat, which is cut and dried and burnt.
traits: holds many times its weight in water; turns water acid; builds and becomes peat; pale spongy head; bog
name: peat + moss
why: Chinese ni tan xian is peat moss. The corpus had it sharing the word sage with Salvia, which is the sage, and peat is both what the moss makes and what it is cut for.

described: Tall tufted grass of dry and salted ground, with a stiff upright spike of paired spikelets and long straight awns standing out from it like bristles. Coarse, tough and grazed only when young.
traits: stiff upright spike; long straight awns like bristles; tufted and coarse; dry salted ground
name: bristle + rye
why: The awns are long and stiff enough to catch on clothing, which is how the plant is met. Sand rye is already Leymus, so the awn does the separating.

described: Fern whose frond divides once into long narrow straps spreading from the top of a wiry black stalk like an opened fan or a bird's spread tail. The spores run in an unbroken line under the rolled edge of each strap.
traits: frond spreading like a fan or tail; long narrow straps; wiry dark stalk; spores in a line under the rolled edge
name: fan + fern
why: Chinese feng wei jue is phoenix tail fern and the spread is exactly that. The corpus was reading pig mane phoenix tail fern, five roots and two animals for one fern.

described: Bracken. A single tall stalk from a deep running rhizome opens into one huge coarse triangular frond, and the plant covers whole hillsides in an unbroken waist-high sheet that shades out everything under it.
traits: one huge coarse triangular frond per stalk; deep running rhizome; covers whole hillsides; waist high
name: hill + fern
why: It is met as terrain rather than as a plant: a hillside under bracken is a different place to walk. That scale is what separates it from every other fern here.

described: Break a stem and a thick white milk wells out that blisters skin and will blind an eye it touches. The plants look nothing alike, weeds, cactus-shaped trees, poinsettias, and what they share is that milk and a tiny false flower built of several real ones crowded into a cup.
traits: caustic white milky latex that blisters and blinds; false flower built of many in a cup; shapes from weed to tree
name: burn + milk
why: The latex is the one thing true of every species in an enormous and otherwise unlike genus, and it is a warning worth carrying in the name. The corpus reduced the Latin to name.

described: Tall club-rush standing in shallow water, stems triangular or round with a loose cluster of brown spikelets near the top. The stems are cut, dried and woven flat into mats, seats and baskets.
traits: cut and woven into mats and seats; stands in shallow water; brown spikelets near the tip; tall stems
name: mat + rush
why: Weaving is why these stems are cut and carried home, and it separates this from the rush whose pith was drawn for a wick and from the sedges beside it.

described: Wiry stiff rush of bog and wet heath, its stems dark and tough, carrying a small tight head of near-black shining spikelets that shows dark against pale bog grasses.
traits: near-black shining spikelets; wiry stiff dark stem; bog and wet heath; small tight head
name: black + rush
why: The blackness of the head against the pale grass is what picks it out at a distance, and it needs a word of its own beside the wick rush and the mat rush.

described: Climber or shrub of warm country with showy brushes of stamens, whose fruit carries four or five stiff papery wings set around it like the sails of a windmill, so that it spins as it falls.
traits: fruit with four or five papery wings; spins as it falls; brush of stamens; climber or shrub
name: spin + seed
why: Chinese feng che zi is windmill seed. A seed that turns on the way down is rare enough to name by and is nothing like a rush, which is what the corpus had it sharing.

described: Evergreen shrub of the tea kin with small leathery toothed leaves set in two flat ranks along the twig, and tiny greenish-white flowers whose smell is strong and distinctly unpleasant, carrying some way on a still day.
traits: strong unpleasant flower smell; small leathery toothed leaf in two flat ranks; tiny greenish flower; black berry
name: stink + shrub
why: The smell reaches a person before the shrub is identified and is the one memorable thing about an otherwise plain evergreen. Wide, which the Latin gives, says nothing at all.

described: Water plant whose round floating leaf grows to the span of two arms, quilted into ridges and studded on BOTH faces with sharp spines, as is the stalk and the flower bud. Purple flowers push up through it, and the seeds are dried and popped as food.
traits: enormous quilted round floating leaf; sharp spines on both leaf faces and the stalk; purple flower; seeds popped as food
name: spine + lily
why: A waterlily covered in spines is unmistakable and the spines are what anyone reaching for it finds first. It cannot share the word wide with Eurya, which is a dry-land shrub.

described: Alpine composite of the high Himalaya whose large flower head hangs face DOWN on a curved woolly stalk, sheltering the florets from rain and cold, so that the plant looks bowed even in full flower.
traits: flower head hanging face down; curved woolly stalk; high alpine; large single head
name: nod + flower
why: Chinese chui tou ju is nodding-head chrysanthemum. The bowed head is unlike anything beside it on the mountain and was coming out as creme wagtail hatred, which is not a plant.

described: Shrub of slender arching twigs that in flower disappear under dense flat or domed heads of tiny white or pink flowers, so thick along the branch that the whole shrub looks like breaking surf.
traits: tiny flowers in dense flat or domed heads; slender arching twig; foams white along the whole branch; small toothed leaf
name: foam + flower
why: The massed flower along an arching branch really does read as foam, and it is how the shrub is recognised at a distance. Privet, which the corpus gave, is Ligustrum.

described: Evergreen shrub with glossy opposite leaves, cut and clipped into dense hedges wherever a boundary is wanted. Loose panicles of small white flowers with a heavy sweet smell that many find sickly, then black berries.
traits: clipped into dense hedges; glossy opposite evergreen leaf; heavy sweet white flower; black berry
name: hedge + shrub
why: It is the hedge plant, grown almost entirely for that and shaped by it, and the use is what everyone who meets it is doing to it.

described: The common grass of meadow and lawn, soft flat leaves whose tips fold into the shape of a small boat, loosely tufted, with an open delicate branching head. It is what a field of grass is mostly made of.
traits: boat-shaped leaf tip; soft flat leaf; open delicate branching head; the common grass of meadow and lawn
name: meadow + grass
why: It is the grass of grassland, and saying so places it exactly. Bare grass was shared with three other genera, which left none of the four with a name.

described: Fine-leaved grass making a soft close turf, with a flowering head so finely branched that from a distance it reads as a haze of purple-grey over the ground rather than as separate stems.
traits: extremely fine branching head like a haze; very fine leaf; close soft turf
name: fine + grass
why: The fineness is the whole character, in leaf, in stem and in the head, and it is what a hand laid on the turf feels.

described: Grass carrying a dense cylindrical spike, stiff and blunt-ended and as thick as a finger, standing up like a cat's tail above the leaves. Cut and dried, it is the best of hay.
traits: dense stiff cylindrical spike like a cat's tail; blunt end; cut for the best hay
name: tail + grass
why: The spike is a tail in shape, thickness and stiffness, and it is the one grass head anyone can name at a glance across a hayfield.

described: Great bulb, often half out of the sand, with long thick strap leaves sprawling from it and an umbel of large white trumpet flowers on a solid stalk, opening at evening with a heavy sweet scent. Coast, riverbank and swamp edge.
traits: great bulb half out of the sand; long thick strap leaves; umbel of large white trumpets; evening scent; coast and riverbank
name: shore + lily
why: It is the lily of sand and the water's edge, which is where it is met and what separates it from Lilium, the lily of the hill and the wood.

described: Low succulent of bare rock, wall and roof, its small leaves swollen thick with water and packed along short stems, with flat heads of star flowers. It grows where there is no soil to speak of and survives being pulled up and left lying.
traits: leaves swollen thick with water; bare rock, wall and roof; flat head of star flowers; survives with almost no soil
name: thick + leaf
why: The leaf is thick to the point that it is the whole plant, and it is what the fingers find. Houseleek, which the corpus offered, is a different plant that already owns the word.

described: Tree with glossy leathery leaves and a large orange fruit sitting in a stiff four-lobed cap, so astringent while firm that it dries the mouth, and honey-sweet once it goes soft. The heartwood of some is black, heavy and sinks in water.
traits: large orange fruit in a stiff four-lobed cap; mouth-drying until soft; black heavy heartwood that sinks
name: cap + fruit
why: The stiff lobed cap stays on the fruit through picking, drying and selling, which is how it is always seen. The Latin means the god's fruit and was coming out as October wheat.

described: Tiny crucifer of high rock and arctic gravel, making a dense hard cushion of small hairy rosettes packed tight against the cold, with a few small white or yellow four-petalled flowers on short stalks just clear of it.
traits: dense hard cushion of small rosettes; high rock and arctic gravel; hairy small leaf; four-petalled flower just clear of the cushion
name: cushion + cress
why: The cushion is a shape the cold forces on it and is how it is found, as a hard pad on bare rock. Whitetop was shared with two unrelated genera.

described: Crucifer of rock ledge and scree, taller and looser than a cushion, with clasping grey-green leaves up the stem and a loose head of four-petalled white flowers, then long narrow flat pods.
traits: rock ledge and scree; clasping grey-green stem leaves; loose head of white four-petal flowers; long flat pods
name: rock + cress
why: Rock cress is already its English name and it places the plant against the cushion cress of the high gravel, which is the neighbour it is most confused with.

described: Small orchid riding on bark, its lip swollen underneath into a deep rounded POUCH that holds nectar, set below a flat spreading front that is usually spotted. Short fleshy leaves in two ranks along a creeping stem.
traits: lip swollen into a deep rounded pouch; spotted flat front to the lip; short fleshy leaves in two ranks; lives on bark
name: pouch + orchid
why: Chinese pen ju lan is basin-spur orchid and the Latin means belly lip. Both name the pouch, which is the one feature that tells it from the orchids around it.

described: Sedge of wet open ground, dense brown spikelets held in a loose umbel on slender stems that never stand still, the whole stand shifting together in the least wind. The style is fringed with fine hairs and drops away once the seed sets.
traits: swaying slender stems; brown spikelet in a loose umbel; fringed style; wet open ground
name: sway + grass
why: Fringe plus sedge came out eighteen letters, because sedge is itself marsh grass. The Chinese piao fu cao names the swaying, which is shorter, seen from further off and just as true.

described: Laurel-family shrub or small tree of the warm south, leaves smooth and strongly aromatic when crushed, carrying its flowers singly or in twos in the leaf joints rather than in the usual cluster.
traits: flowers borne singly, not in clusters; strongly aromatic crushed leaf; laurel kin; warm south
name: lone + laurel
why: The corpus reads it as willow, which is Salix and owns that word. Flowering one at a time is what its Chinese name picks out and what separates it in its own family.

described: Bamboo with one branch at each node and long tough culm sheaths that stay wrapped on the cane for years instead of falling, so an old cane is still half clothed in them.
traits: sheaths that stay on the cane for years; one branch per node; upright cane; warm temperate
name: sheath + bamboo
why: Arrow bamboo is already Fargesia and this one is equally straight, so the clinging sheath does the separating and is visible on every old cane.

described: Orchid with two broad soft pleated leaves rising from a small bulb, and the leaves look oiled, catching light with a greasy sheen unlike the matt leaves around them. A loose raceme of small greenish or dull purple flowers.
traits: leaves with a greasy oiled sheen; two broad pleated leaves; small bulb; small dull flowers
name: shine + orchid
why: The Latin liparos is greasy and the sheen is real and odd enough to find it by in shade. River, which the corpus gave, belongs to nothing about the plant.

described: Succulent of dry stony ground with fleshy leaves scattered along upright stems, and small starry flowers in a loose head, taller and looser than the mats and cushions of true stonecrop.
traits: fleshy leaves up an upright stem; taller and looser than stonecrop; dry stony ground; loose head of star flowers
name: false + thick + leaf
why: It is named against the stonecrop and looks like it until the stems go up instead of out, so the name has to carry both the likeness and the difference.

described: Orchid whose lip is folded into a deep hollow SHOE, waxy and often veined, with a stiff shield above it and a pair of drooping side petals. The leaves are strap-like and usually mottled in two greens. One flower to a stem.
traits: lip folded into a deep hollow shoe; mottled strap leaves; stiff shield above the lip; one flower per stem
name: shoe + orchid
why: Slipper orchid is its name in every language that has one, and the shoe is unmistakable. Pouch is already Gastrochilus, whose lip is a rounded sac rather than a shoe.

described: Wiry herb of woodland shade with thin leathery heart-shaped leaflets edged in fine spines, and sprays of small spidery flowers drawn out into long slender spurs. It is dug and dried as the famous goat herb.
traits: heart-shaped leaflets edged with fine spines; spidery flower with long spurs; woodland shade; the goat herb
name: goat + herb
why: Chinese yin yang huo names it for what it does to goats, which is why it is gathered and why everyone who knows it knows it. Plant, which the corpus gave, says nothing.

described: Crucifer with huge coarse dock-like leaves and a long thick white taproot. Grate the root and the heat is immediate and goes straight up behind the nose and into the eyes, quite unlike the warm heat of ginger.
traits: long thick white taproot; heat that goes up the nose; huge coarse leaves; grated fresh
name: nose + root
why: The burn is in the nose rather than the mouth, which is what tells it from ginger, and the root is the whole plant as far as anyone using it is concerned.

described: Low sprawling herb with opposite toothed leaves and small flat four-lobed flowers of an intense sky blue, each with a pale eye at its centre. The seed case is flattened and notched into a heart.
traits: intense sky-blue flat flower; pale eye at the centre; four lobes; flattened heart-shaped seed case
name: blue + eye
why: The blue with a pale centre is the plant, seen from standing height in a lawn. The corpus was giving female name, which is a dictionary admitting it does not know.

described: Tall soft grass whose large spikelets hang and nod on fine stalks, each one drawn out into long straight awns, and whose leaf sheaths are soft and hairy to the hand.
traits: large nodding hanging spikelets; long straight awns; soft hairy leaf sheath; tall and soft
name: bird + oat
why: Chinese que mai is sparrow wheat, which places it beside the oat it resembles and apart from it. Oat alone belongs to Avena.

described: Flowers open as a five-pointed star with a tight cone of yellow anthers standing in the middle, and the fruit is a berry. Potato, tomato, aubergine and the deadly nightshades are all built this way, and most of the green parts will make a person ill.
traits: five-pointed star flower; cone of yellow anthers at the centre; berry; green parts poisonous
name: star + berry
why: The star with its yellow cone and then a berry is the whole enormous genus in one look, from the potato to the nightshade, and no neighbour does it.

described: Liana climbing on hooked tendrils, with three-veined leaves and a hard round fruit like an orange holding flat grey seeds. Those seeds carry the poison that is smeared on darts and that kills by locking every muscle at once.
traits: seeds carrying a dart poison; climbs on hooked tendrils; three-veined leaf; hard round fruit
name: dart + poison
why: The poison is why the plant was ever sought, carried and traded, and a name that says so is a name worth having. Nightshade belongs to Solanum.

described: Shrub with opposite toothed leaves that in autumn carries tight clusters of berries packed along the stem in a violet so bright and so purple that nothing else in the wood is that colour.
traits: clusters of brilliant violet berries packed along the stem; opposite toothed leaf; autumn
name: purple + bead
why: Chinese zi zhu is purple bead. The colour is genuinely unlike anything else growing and is what the shrub is planted and remembered for. The Latin means beautiful fruit and was being read as tame ape.

described: Woody vine with big heart-shaped leaves, climbing high into trees, hung with egg-shaped fruits covered in short brown fur. Cut one and the flesh is vivid green or gold around a pale core ringed with tiny black seeds.
traits: brown furry skin; vivid green flesh with a ring of black seeds; big heart-shaped leaf; woody climber
name: fur + fruit
why: The fur on the skin is the first thing a hand finds and the thing that makes the fruit unmistakable. The corpus was reading macaque monkey twice over for one vine.

described: Tall woodland herb whose large leaves are cut into stiff angular lobes, broad and flattened and notched so that each reads as the shell of a crab. Small pale flower heads in a loose open spike above them.
traits: leaf cut into stiff angular lobes like a crab shell; tall woodland herb; small pale heads in a loose spike
name: crab + leaf
why: Chinese xie jia cao is crab shell grass and the leaf really does read as one. Beside, which the corpus gave, is the Latin prefix alone with the rest of the word dropped.

described: Low herb of wet ground and stream side with rounded kidney-shaped leaves held flat near the ground on long stalks, and flat heads of small yellow daisies on upright stems above them.
traits: rounded kidney-shaped basal leaf; wet ground and stream side; flat head of small yellow daisies
name: round + leaf + daisy
why: The round basal leaf is what is seen before the flower and what tells it from the ragged-leaved daisies it grows among. The corpus gave sinus, the prefix alone.

described: Aroid of field edge and waste ground with leaves split into three, and a narrow green hood from which the spadix runs out and up into a long thin whip, far longer than the hood itself. The small round tuber is acrid raw and is dried for sickness and phlegm.
traits: spadix drawn into a long thin whip beyond the hood; leaf split into three; small round acrid tuber
name: whip + hood
why: The whip standing out well beyond the hood is unlike the cobra hood of Arisaema beside it, and it is the character the plant is picked out by.

described: Shrub whose leaves are covered in minute star-shaped hairs that make both faces feel like fine sandpaper, hung in season with masses of pure white starry flowers. The older twigs are hollow.
traits: leaves rough as sandpaper from star-shaped hairs; masses of white starry flowers; hollow twigs
name: rough + leaf
why: The roughness is felt the moment a leaf is touched and is on every species. Misuse plus einkorn, which the corpus gave, is two wrong guesses joined.

described: Tiny alpine making a tight mat or cushion of small rosettes on bare high ground, scattered over with small flat white or pink flowers each with a yellow or red eye, held just clear on short stalks like dots on the ground.
traits: small flat flowers dotted over a tight cushion; yellow or red eye; bare high ground; tiny rosettes
name: ground + star
why: Chinese dian di mei is dot-ground plum, for flowers scattered across the surface. Unknown plant, which the corpus gave, is the dictionary shrugging, and forty-five species were sharing that shrug.

described: Evergreen with thick leathery toothed leaves that catch the light like polished leather, and whose new growth flushes a brilliant red that holds for weeks. Flat heads of small white flowers with a rank smell, then red berries.
traits: leaves glossy as polished leather; new growth flushing brilliant red; flat head of rank-smelling white flowers; red berry
name: shine + leaf
why: The Latin photeinos is shining and the leaf is genuinely polished-looking. Stone plus name-of-tree, which the corpus gave, is half a place and half an admission of ignorance.

described: Minute pale green leafy liverwort spreading as a thin film over bark and over the surface of living leaves in wet forest, so fine that it reads as a bloom or a stain until a lens shows the overlapping shoots.
traits: spreads as a thin film over bark and living leaves; minute and pale green; reads as a stain until magnified; wet forest
name: film + moss
why: Growing as a film on the surface of other leaves is unusual enough to name by, and it separates this from the ear-pouched and feathered liverworts beside it.

described: Bog and wet meadow herb with a rosette of heart-shaped leaves flat on the ground, and one white flower to a stalk, its five petals veined with fine green lines and set around five fringed golden bodies that glisten like drops of nectar but hold none.
traits: single white flower per stalk; petals veined with green lines; fringed golden false stamens; heart-shaped basal rosette; wet meadow
name: plum + flower
why: Chinese mei hua cao is plum-flower grass, and the flat open five-petalled white flower really does read as plum blossom held low over a bog. Hymettus, which the corpus gave, is a mountain in Attica.

described: Low herb of shaded wet limestone in the far south, with opposite leaves and small white or pink tubular flowers set along a branch that COILS back on itself like a snail shell, opening one flower at a time from the outside in.
traits: flower branch coiled like a snail shell; small tubular white or pink flower; shaded wet limestone; low herb
name: coil + flower
why: Chinese luo xu cao names the spiral order of the flowers, which is the one thing that marks it out among a great many small white-flowered herbs of the same rock.

described: Thistle with spiny wings running down the stem and leaves cut into spine-tipped lobes, carrying a head of purple florets. When it seeds, each seed hangs from a pappus of hairs that are themselves feathered along their length.
traits: pappus hairs feathered along their length; spiny wings down the stem; purple floret head; spine-tipped leaf lobes
name: plume + thistle
why: Thistle alone was shared with Carduus, whose seed hairs are plain. The feathered pappus is the character that separates the two genera in every key.

described: Legume whose pod swells into a dry papery bladder while the seeds inside shrink away from the wall, so that a ripe pod shaken in the hand rattles like a small gourd. Yellow pea flowers, often with a keel drawn to a twisted beak.
traits: pod inflates into a papery bladder; loose seeds rattle when shaken; yellow pea flower; twisted keel
name: rattle + pod
why: The Latin crotalon is a rattle and Chinese xiang ling dou is ringing-bell bean. It is a test a child performs on meeting the plant and it works on every species.

described: Spiny tree with pinnate leaves held up to the light showing them dotted all over with clear oil glands. The dried husk on the tongue is not simply hot: it buzzes and goes numb, a tingling that spreads and lasts, over a smell of lemon peel.
traits: husk that makes the tongue buzz and go numb; clear oil dots through the leaf; spines on trunk and twig; lemon-peel smell
name: numb + pepper
why: Nothing else in food does what it does to the mouth, so the sensation names it exactly and unmistakably. Zeus bird timber, which the corpus gave, is a god and two guesses.

described: Leafy liverwort pressed so flat against bark or rock that the shoot reads as a single ribbon, each leaf carrying a small flat lobe folded tight under it against the stem. Thin dark mats, closely applied to the surface.
traits: shoot flattened to a ribbon; leaves pressed flat to the surface; small flat lobe folded under each leaf; thin dark mat
name: flat + moss
why: Flatness is what the Latin scraper was reaching for and is what the hand and eye both find first. It separates it from the feathered, eared and filmy liverworts already named.

described: Low creeping herb carpeting wet shade and stream sides, with small rounded scalloped leaves. The flowers have NO petals at all, and instead the leaves immediately around them turn a bright golden green, so that a whole patch glows yellow from a distance.
traits: no petals at all; leaves around the flower turning bright golden green; rounded scalloped leaf; wet shade and stream side; forms carpets
name: gold + leaf
why: The gold is in the leaf because there is no petal to put it in, which is unusual enough to name by, and the Chinese jin yao names the same gold. Spleenwort is a fern and has nothing to do with it.

described: Mint-family herb of forest shade with a square stem, wrinkled opposite leaves and whorls of white or pale pink two-lipped flowers ringing the stem at intervals, shorter and softer than its open-ground relative.
traits: flowers in rings around a square stem; forest shade; white or pale pink two-lipped flower; wrinkled opposite leaf
name: false + ring + flower
why: It is named against Phlomoides and looks like it, so the name has to carry the likeness and the difference. The corpus was giving beside, the prefix alone with the rest dropped.

described: Orchid of the ground rather than the tree, with strongly pleated ribbed leaves up the stem and a flower whose lip is blown up into a deep hollow bowl like a ladle, held under a spreading hood with two twisted ribbons hanging at the sides.
traits: lip swollen into a deep ladle-shaped bowl; strongly pleated ribbed leaves; twisted side petals; grows in the ground
name: spoon + orchid
why: Chinese shao lan is ladle orchid and the pouch is rounded and open like one. Shoe is already Paphiopedilum, whose lip is a closed slipper, and the two are told apart exactly there.
