described: Tree or scrambling shrub whose leaf is divided into seven or nine leaflets all spreading from the top of one long stalk, so that each leaf reads as a webbed foot or an open umbrella held above the branch.
traits: leaflets spreading from one point like a webbed foot; seven to nine leaflets; long leaf stalk; tree or scrambler
name: goose + foot
why: Chinese e zhang chai is goose-foot firewood and the spread of leaflets is exactly a goose's foot. Seven leaf is already Aesculus, whose leaflets are broad and blunt rather than webbed.

described: Laurel-family shrub whose leaves and young twigs, scratched or broken, give off a strong warm spice smell with lemon behind it. Small yellow flowers come on bare wood before the leaves, then glossy black berries.
traits: strong spice and lemon smell from scratched twig and leaf; yellow flowers on bare wood before the leaves; glossy black berry
name: spice + bush
why: Spicebush is already its English name and the smell is the plant: nothing else in the wood answers to a scratched twig that way. Lindos is an island and mistress is a guess.

described: Herb of shaded limestone in the warm south, opposite hairy leaves, pale purple or white two-lipped tubular flowers, and a long straight slender capsule that dries and splits lengthwise into two halves which then twist apart like a wrung cloth.
traits: long straight slender capsule; the two halves twist apart on splitting; opposite hairy leaf; shaded limestone; two-lipped tubular flower
name: twist + pod
why: The twisting capsule is the character the genus is keyed on and is still there on a dried plant months later. Its neighbours on the same rock are already named by cliff and bell and trumpet.

described: Tree, shrub or vine with big glossy veined leaves, whose fruit is many berries fused into one lumpy pale body with a warty surface. Ripe, it smells strongly and unmistakably of rancid cheese, and it is drunk as a tonic all the same. The root gives a red dye.
traits: fruit of fused berries with a lumpy warty surface; powerful rancid cheese smell when ripe; red dye from the root; glossy veined leaf
name: stink + fruit
why: The smell reaches a person across a clearing and is what everyone who has met the fruit remembers. Stink shrub is Eurya, a dry-land evergreen, so the pair are never confused.

described: Small ginger of forest shade whose flower spike arches over and hangs, the yellow or orange flowers held far out on long slender curved stalks so that they bob and turn at the least movement of air.
traits: flowers on long slender curved stalks that bob in any air; arching hanging spike; yellow or orange; small forest ginger
name: dance + ginger
why: Chinese wu hua jiang is dancing-flower ginger and the movement is genuinely the thing seen first, the flowers turning while the rest of the plant is still.

described: Herb of alpine turf and dry steppe with leaves cut into fine feathery threads, and a single cup-shaped flower held above them, glossy enough to catch the sun, brilliant yellow or blood red, opening while the ground is still cold.
traits: single glossy cup-shaped flower; brilliant yellow or blood red; leaves cut to fine feathery threads; opens early on cold ground
name: gold + cup
why: Chinese ce jin zhan hua is side golden-cup flower. The flower is cupped, lacquer-bright and solitary, which is the whole plant at a distance.

described: Crucifer of ditch, wet field and pond edge, with lyre-shaped or deeply cut leaves and small four-petalled yellow flowers, then short curved pods. The leaf is peppery and is picked and eaten.
traits: wet ditch and field edge; small yellow four-petal flower; lyre-shaped cut leaf; peppery edible leaf; short curved pod
name: wet + cress
why: It is the cress of standing water, which places it exactly against the cushion cress of high gravel and the rock cress of dry ledges already named.

described: Succulent of rock and roadside with FLAT toothed fleshy leaves rather than the swollen cylinders of true stonecrop, in flat heads of yellow star flowers. The young leaves are gathered and cooked as a vegetable.
traits: flat toothed fleshy leaf, not cylindrical; flat head of yellow star flowers; rock and roadside; young leaves eaten
name: flat + thick + leaf
why: Thick leaf is Sedum, whose leaves are swollen into cylinders. This one is thick and flat at once, which is exactly the difference and exactly what the hand finds.

described: Sprawling herb whose flowers push out of a folded boat-shaped bract, each with TWO large bright blue petals standing up like ears and a third small and pale below. A flower opens at dawn and is gone by noon.
traits: two large blue petals and one small pale one; flower lasts a single morning; folded boat-shaped bract; sprawling succulent stem
name: day + flower
why: The flower lasts one morning and the plant is named for it in every language. Blue, which is what is seen, is shared with too much else to carry the name alone.

described: Shrub whose slender bare twigs hang, through the last of winter, long stiff drooping spikes of pale yellow bell flowers set in even rows, like strings of beads or a row of small lanterns, all before a single leaf opens.
traits: long stiff drooping flower spikes on bare wood; pale yellow bells in even rows; flowers before the leaves; late winter
name: hang + spike
why: The Latin means spike tail and the spikes hang from bare twigs in the dead of the year, which is when the shrub is seen and the only time it can be mistaken for nothing else.

described: Legume whose flat pod is jointed into segments, each segment covered in minute hooked hairs so that the pod breaks apart on contact and every piece rides away on wool, fur or a trouser leg.
traits: pod jointed into segments; segments covered in minute hooked hairs; breaks apart and sticks to anything passing
name: cling + pod
why: Chinese na shen cao is grab-body grass. The plant is met by being carried off by it, usually noticed hours later, and no other pod here does that.

described: Umbellifer of high alpine meadow with aromatic leaves cut into fine divisions and flat white umbels, over a thick strongly aromatic rhizome that is dug, dried and simmered for aching joints and cold in the bones.
traits: thick aromatic rhizome dug for aching joints; high alpine meadow; finely cut aromatic leaf; flat white umbel
name: ache + root
why: The root is what is dug, carried and sold, and what it is taken for is the ache. It sits beside the bitter, hot, dark and rose roots and is told apart from all of them by use.

described: Small moss making thin dull green mats over tree bases and damp rock in shaded woodland, the shoots creeping and the branches short and erect, the whole growth so slight it reads as a stain until touched.
traits: thin dull green creeping mat; short erect branches; tree bases and damp rock; shaded woodland
name: thin + moss
why: Chinese bao luo xian is thin-gauze moss. Thinness is what it is, and it separates it from the feathered, eared, filmy and flattened liverworts already named.

described: Fast soft-wooded legume of wet field and paddy edge, with long pinnate leaves of many small paired leaflets, yellow pea flowers often flecked purple, and very long thin pods hanging straight down like cords.
traits: very long thin hanging pods; many small paired leaflets; wet field and paddy edge; grows fast and is dug in to feed the soil
name: long + pod
why: The pods hang a hand's length and straight, which is visible from across a field and is unlike the rattling bladder and the clinging joints of the other pods named.

described: Stout tall grass with broad maize-like leaves, carrying at the top a dense head of hard reddish-brown grain. It stands drought that kills other grain, is ground for flour and porridge, and is fermented for the strong clear liquor.
traits: tall stout stem with broad leaves; dense head of reddish-brown grain; stands drought; ground for flour, fermented for liquor
name: tall + grain
why: Chinese gao liang is tall grain. It stands head and shoulders above the other cereals in a field and the grain is the point of it.

described: Small tree armed on trunk and branch with long stiff thorns that themselves branch into more thorns, with glossy toothed leaves and small dark red-purple plum-like fruits that are sweet-sour and eaten fresh. Planted in rows as a hedge nothing will push through.
traits: long branched thorns on trunk and branch; planted as a stockproof hedge; small dark red plum-like fruit; glossy toothed leaf
name: thorn + hedge
why: Chinese ci li mu is thorn-hedge tree, which is what it is grown for and what its branched thorns make possible. Hedge shrub is Ligustrum, which is clipped and has no thorns at all.

described: Tree with leaves rough as sandpaper, funnel-shaped white or orange flowers, and a fruit whose pulp is clear, sticky and stringy enough to be used as paste for paper and as a glue. The young fruit is pickled and eaten.
traits: fruit pulp sticky enough to use as glue; leaves rough as sandpaper; funnel-shaped flower; young fruit pickled
name: glue + fruit
why: The pulp really is used as paste and that use is old and widespread. It is also the one thing about the fruit a person discovers immediately, by finding their fingers stuck together.

described: Moss of high cold rock and the edges of late snow, in dense dark tufts whose narrow leaves are all curved and swept to one side, so that a cushion looks combed by a wind that is no longer blowing.
traits: leaves all swept to one side; dense dark tuft; high cold rock and snowbed edges; narrow curved leaf
name: sweep + moss
why: Every leaf lying the same way makes the tuft look brushed, which is visible with the naked eye and is what separates it on the bare rock where it grows.

described: Thick fleshy cane carrying large leaves boldly blotched and streaked in cream over deep green. The sap is loaded with fine needle crystals, and a mouthful swells the tongue and throat so that a person cannot speak for days.
traits: sap that swells the tongue and stops speech; large leaves blotched cream over green; thick fleshy cane; deep shade
name: mute + cane
why: Being struck dumb by it is the reason it has the name it has in English, and a name that carries the warning is worth more than one that describes the blotches.

described: Legume shrub with leaves divided into many tiny paired leaflets that fold shut when touched or at dusk, and flower heads that are a half-sphere of long silky stamens, scarlet or white, standing out like a powder puff or a shaving brush.
traits: flower head a half-sphere of long silky stamens; scarlet or white; many tiny paired leaflets that fold shut; shrub
name: brush + flower
why: The flower has no visible petals worth the name, only the brush of stamens, and that is both the whole appearance and the reason it is planted.

described: Tufted grass of dry thin turf with a dense narrow spike-like head, tight and cylindrical, which catches the light along its whole length and shines silver as it dries.
traits: dense narrow cylindrical head that shines silver; tufted; dry thin turf; tight spike-like panicle
name: silver + spike
why: The shine on a dried head picks it out of a dry sward from some distance, and the head is tight and spike-like where its relatives are open and airy.

described: Tree with enormous corrugated leaves whose strong parallel veins run straight to a toothed edge, large white or yellow flowers, and a hard green fruit made not of a wall but of the fleshy sepals closing over the seeds. Sour, and cooked into curry.
traits: enormous corrugated leaf with strong parallel veins; fruit made of fleshy sepals closing over the seeds; hard, green and sour; cooked in curry
name: elephant + apple
why: Elephant apple is its name across South Asia, for the size and hardness of the fruit and for what eats it where it falls. The leaf is the other candidate and is shared with several trees beside it.

described: Herb with pinnate leaves and a fruit drawn out into a long straight beak. When the beak dries it splits and each seed comes away with a tail that COILS and uncoils as the air turns damp or dry, walking the sharp seed down into the soil.
traits: fruit drawn into a long beak; seed tail that coils and uncoils with damp; drills itself into the ground; pinnate leaf
name: beak + seed
why: The beaked fruit is on the plant for months and is unmistakable, and the coiling that follows is one of the odder things a seed does. The needle grass drills too, but with a straight awn and no beak.

described: Herb whose leaf is divided into many small leaflets set in even pairs straight up the stalk, so that each leaf reads as a ladder laid on the ground, under loose heads of blue bell flowers.
traits: leaflets in even pairs up the stalk like the rungs of a ladder; loose head of blue bell flowers; herb of meadow and scree
name: ladder + leaf
why: The ladder is what its English name says and what anyone sees in the leaf before they notice the flower. It is a regular, countable arrangement rather than a vague feathery one.

described: Herb of marsh, ditch and pond margin, often half in the water, with narrow opposite leaves crowded at the swollen nodes, sometimes with spines among them, and small purple flowers sitting tight in the leaf joints.
traits: stands in marsh and shallow water; narrow opposite leaves crowded at swollen nodes; spines among the leaves in some; flowers tight in the leaf joints
name: marsh + herb
why: The Latin means water-loving and where it stands is the honest answer, since nothing about the leaf or flower is unusual enough to carry the name on its own.

described: Moss growing on the bark of living trees in tight dark cushions that clothe a trunk or a branch, its leaves pressed in and curled when dry and opening out again in rain.
traits: grows on the bark of living trees; tight dark cushion clothing the trunk; leaves curled when dry, opening in rain
name: bark + moss
why: Chinese mu yi xian is tree-clothing moss. Living on bark rather than on ground or rock is the fact about it, and the cushions really do clothe a trunk.

described: Very small creeping moss making fine thin mats on rock and bark, slighter even than the thin moss it is named against, with minute closely set leaves along thread-like shoots.
traits: finer and thinner than Leskea; thread-like creeping shoots; minute closely set leaves; rock and bark
name: false + thin + moss
why: It is named against the thin moss and is the harder of the two to see, so the name has to carry both the likeness and the fact that this is the lesser of the pair.

described: Tree or scrambling shrub whose leaf divides into seven or nine leaflets spreading from the top of one long stalk, held out over the branch like an opened umbrella and shedding rain the same way.
traits: leaflets spreading from one point like an opened umbrella; seven to nine leaflets; long leaf stalk; tree or scrambler
name: umbrella + leaf
why: Goose foot belongs to Chenopodium, whose Greek name says exactly that and which has the better claim. Umbrella is what this one is called in English and is the same spread seen from below.

described: Weed of waste and cultivated ground with mealy grey-green leaves shaped, broad at the base and lobed to a point, like the webbed foot of a goose, and dense spikes of tiny green flowers. The seed is ground and eaten.
traits: leaf shaped like a webbed goose foot; mealy grey-green bloom on the leaf; dense spikes of tiny green flowers; waste ground; seed ground for food
name: goose + foot
why: The Greek chen podion IS goose foot and the leaf shape is the whole reason for the name, in Latin and in English both.

described: Small ground orchid whose flowers are set in a single rank that TWISTS around the stem as it climbs, so the spike rises as a neat spiral of little white tubular flowers, like a plait.
traits: flowers in one rank spiralling up the stem; small white tubular flowers; neat plaited spike; ground orchid of turf
name: spiral + orchid
why: The spiral is the plant, named for it in Latin and called ladies' tresses in English for the same plait. Coil belongs to Spiradiclis, whose flower BRANCH coils rather than the spike.

described: Small tough fern of dry rock and crevice, fronds finely cut and often scaly or woolly beneath, curled up and apparently dead in drought. The edge of each segment rolls under to make a continuous LIP covering the spores.
traits: frond edge rolled under into a lip over the spores; small and tough; dry rock crevice; scaly or woolly beneath; curls up in drought
name: lip + fern
why: The rolled lip is what the Greek names and is the character the genus is keyed on. Lip flower is Justicia, and the fern keeps the two apart.

described: Legume shrub or stiff herb with trifoliate leaves and small purple-pink pea flowers in the leaf joints, on stems so tough and wiry they are cut and bound into brooms and woven into coarse baskets.
traits: stems tough and wiry enough for brooms and baskets; trifoliate leaf; small purple-pink pea flower; binds poor soil
name: wire + bush
why: The stems are the useful part and their stiffness is what is felt on grasping the plant. The flowers are small and shared with half the legumes around it.

described: Evergreen shrub with stiff pinnate leaves whose leaflets are edged with hard holly spines, upright racemes of yellow flowers, and drooping bunches of blue-black berries with a grey bloom that look like small grapes. The inner wood is bright yellow.
traits: holly-spined leaflets on a pinnate leaf; bunches of blue-black berries with a bloom; yellow inner wood; upright yellow flower racemes
name: holly + grape
why: Both halves are what it is called in English, and together they say the leaf and the fruit at once. Yellow thorn is Berberis, which shares the yellow wood but has simple leaves and real thorns.

described: Delicate tufted grass whose flowering head opens into a wide airy spray of many tiny flattened spikelets on hair-fine branches, so that from a few paces the whole head reads as a haze standing over the ground.
traits: very open airy head of tiny flattened spikelets; hair-fine branches; reads as a haze at a distance; tufted
name: cloud + grass
why: The head is open to the point of being more air than plant, which separates it from the tight spike of Koeleria and the tail of Phleum. Fine grass is already Agrostis.

described: Gesneriad hanging from rock face and tree trunk, with thick toothed leaves set in whorls of three along woody stems, and pale purple tubular flowers with a flared mouth drooping clear of the rock.
traits: hangs from rock face and tree trunk; thick toothed leaves in whorls of three; pale purple tubular flower; woody stem
name: hang + trumpet
why: Chinese diao shi ju tai is hanging-stone gesneriad. Hanging clear of the surface is what tells it from the cliff rosettes of Oreocharis and Primulina, which press flat against it.

described: Marsh and shallow-water plant with a rosette of soft translucent grassy leaves below the surface, sending up thin twisted bare stalks each topped by one small hard grey-white BUTTON of tiny crowded flowers, like a pin stuck in the water.
traits: one hard grey-white button of flowers per stalk; thin twisted bare stalk; rosette of translucent grassy leaves; shallow water
name: button + stalk
why: The button on a bare stalk is the whole plant above water and is unlike anything growing with it. Woolly stalk, which the Greek says, describes the hairs on the button rather than the stalk.

described: Moss of bare damp soil and bank, shoots glossy and often reddish at the base, with long-necked capsules hanging over on curved stalks. Many kinds carry small hard bulbils tucked in the leaf joints that break off and grow.
traits: hard bulbils in the leaf joints that break off and grow; glossy shoots, reddish below; long-necked hanging capsule; bare damp soil
name: bud + moss
why: The bulbils are how it spreads and how it is told from its neighbours under a lens, and they are on the plant whether or not it has fruited.

described: Thick dark strap leaves standing in a stiff rosette straight from the ground, holding their colour through frost and drought year after year, with a short dense spike of pale fleshy flowers low among the leaf bases and then red berries.
traits: holds dark green through frost and drought for years; thick stiff strap leaves in a rosette; dense short flower spike at ground level; red berries
name: ever + green
why: Chinese wan nian qing is ten-thousand-year green, and lasting is the whole point of the plant and the reason it is grown and given. Winter green is Ilex, which is a woody shrub with spined leaves.

described: Small creeping herb spreading over wet mud and the drying edges of ponds and paddy, with small opposite leaves and tiny two-lipped white or purple flowers sitting singly in the leaf joints.
traits: creeps over wet mud and drying pond edges; small opposite leaves; tiny two-lipped flower alone in the leaf joint; low mat
name: mud + herb
why: Where it grows is the only distinctive thing about a very small and very plain plant, and it grows on bare wet mud where almost nothing else creeps.

described: Climbing palm whose stem is solid, immensely long and flexible, running a hundred paces through the canopy. It climbs on whips thrown out beyond the leaves and armed along their length with backward-curving hooks that catch and hold. The stripped cane is the rattan of chairs and rope.
traits: climbs on whips armed with backward hooks; solid immensely long flexible stem; stripped for rattan cane and rope; spiny throughout
name: hook + cane
why: The hooks are how it climbs and how it catches anyone walking under it, and the cane is why it is cut. Reed belongs to the true reeds, which are hollow and stand on their own.

described: Fleshy herb creeping flat over wet shaded ground and rock, its stems rooting as they go, the leaves markedly lopsided and often banded or mottled with silver along the veins.
traits: creeps flat and roots as it goes; markedly lopsided leaf; silver banding along the veins; wet shade
name: crawl + leaf
why: It is met as a mat on the ground rather than as a plant standing up, which is what separates it from the upright Elatostema and the translucent-stemmed Pilea beside it.

described: Woody twiner that spirals up a trunk and strangles it, with rounded toothed leaves and, in autumn, round orange capsules that split into three and curl back to show seeds coated in brilliant scarlet, held on the bare stems all winter.
traits: twines and strangles what it climbs; orange capsule splitting to scarlet seed; holds fruit on bare stems all winter; rounded toothed leaf
name: snake + vine
why: Chinese nan she teng is south snake vine, for the way it winds. Holly belongs to Ilex, which is an evergreen shrub with spined leaves and nothing to do with this.

described: Gesneriad of shaded wet rock with opposite toothed leaves and small tubular flowers, whose fruit is a long slender capsule that splits down its length into two equal halves lying side by side like a pair.
traits: capsule splitting into two equal halves lying together; long and slender; opposite toothed leaf; shaded wet rock
name: twin + pod
why: The Greek didymos is twin and names that paired split, which is on the plant long after flowering. Henckelia's halves twist apart instead, which is where the two are told apart.

described: Tall coarse herb with big blunt leaves that taste sharply sour when chewed, and dense spikes of small flowers that ripen into papery brown-red winged fruits, the whole stem turning rust colour and standing through winter.
traits: leaves sharply sour to chew; papery brown-red winged fruit in dense spikes; tall rust-coloured stem standing all winter; big blunt leaf
name: sour + leaf
why: The sourness is immediate, is on every species, and is why the leaves are picked. Sorrel was shared with Melampyrum, which is not sour and is not related.

described: Aromatic herb with deeply lobed leaves that smell sharp and clean when bruised, carrying dense daisy heads that open as the days shorten and the other flowers are finishing, in yellow, white and bronze.
traits: opens as the days shorten, after everything else; aromatic deeply lobed leaf; dense daisy head; yellow, white and bronze
name: autumn + daisy
why: Flowering when the year is closing is the whole reason it is grown, painted and drunk as tea. Gold flower was shared with Helichrysum, whose heads are dry everlastings.

described: Large open cup-shaped flower of five overlapping petals with a long column of fused stamens pushed out through the middle, opening in the morning and finished by night. The bark of some strips into strong fibre.
traits: big open cup of five petals; long stamen column through the centre; flower lasts a single day; strong bark fibre
name: day + cup
why: The flower is a wide shallow cup and it lasts from morning to dusk, both of which anyone meeting the plant sees at once. Marsh mallow is a different plant and was costing fifteen letters.

described: Fir. Flat soft needles set singly on the twig, each with two chalk-white bands underneath, and cones that stand UPRIGHT on the upper branches like candles and never fall whole: they crumble apart on the tree and leave a bare spike standing.
traits: cones standing upright on the branch; cones crumble apart on the tree rather than falling; flat needles with two white bands beneath
name: stand + cone
why: No other conifer holds its cones upright and none sheds them by falling to pieces in place. Silver fir was shared with Cathaya, and silver describes the needle rather than the tree.

described: Small dull green moss of soil, wall and path, forming low turfs, whose spore capsule opens to a ring of fine teeth TWISTED together into a spiral cord that unwinds as it dries and flicks the spores out.
traits: capsule teeth twisted into a spiral that unwinds when dry; small dull green turf; soil, wall and bare path
name: twist + moss
why: Chinese niu kou xian is twisted-mouth moss. The twist is what the genus is keyed on under a lens and it does visible work, winding and unwinding with the weather. Beard was shared with two unrelated genera.

described: Flat rosette pressed to trodden ground, its broad leaves crossed by strong parallel ribs that stand out on the underside and pull out as tough threads when the leaf is torn. A bare stalk carries a dense narrow spike of tiny flowers.
traits: strong parallel ribs standing out on the leaf; ribs pull out as tough threads; flat rosette on trodden ground; dense narrow spike on a bare stalk
name: rib + leaf
why: Ribwort is already one of its English names and the ribs are what a hand finds when tearing a leaf. Plantain was shared with Holosteum and is also the name of a banana.

described: Grass whose flowering head opens wide into a spreading branched spray, each branch ending in a small hard shining grain, round and smooth enough to roll between the fingers. Some kinds are grown for those grains.
traits: head spreading wide into a branched spray; small round shining hard grain; grains grown as food; tufted or sprawling
name: spread + grain
why: The head opens out where its relatives stay tight, and the grain is round and polished rather than long. Millet was shared with Cenchrus and Milium and named none of the three.

described: Umbellifer with leaves cut into narrow segments and flat heads of small white or yellow flowers, over a thick root that smells strongly resinous when cut and is dug, sliced and simmered for a stubborn cough.
traits: thick resinous-smelling root dug for cough; leaves cut into narrow segments; flat white or yellow umbel
name: cough + root
why: Chinese qian hu names the root and the use, and the cough is what it is gathered and sold for. Ache root is Hansenia, taken for joints, and the two are told apart by what they treat.

described: Climbing gourd with heart-shaped leaves, coiling tendrils and bright yellow bell flowers, bearing small oblong gourds that ripen from green through orange to a deep red, hanging singly among the leaves.
traits: small oblong gourd ripening to deep red; heart-shaped leaf; coiling tendril; yellow bell flower
name: red + gourd
why: Chinese chi pao is red gourd. The colour of the ripe fruit hanging in green leaves is what it is found by, and bitter vine is already Hemsleya, whose fruit is not red.

described: Small delicate umbellifer of damp forest floor, leaves divided into fine segments, carrying tiny white flowers whose petals are each hollowed into a small pouch at the base rather than lying flat.
traits: petals hollowed into a small pouch at the base; tiny white flower; finely divided leaf; damp forest floor
name: pouch + petal
why: Chinese nang ban qin is pouch-petal parsley and the Greek says the same. It is the one character that separates a very small plain umbellifer from the others on the same ground.

described: Laurel tree with smooth aromatic leaves whose fruit is a small hard ball, the seed sealed inside a thick woody shell that has to be cracked rather than cut, the flesh around it thin and barely there.
traits: seed sealed in a thick hard woody shell; small hard round fruit; thin flesh; aromatic laurel leaf
name: thick + shell
why: Chinese hou ke gui is thick-shell cassia and the Greek means hidden nut, both naming the same sealed shell. It was costing seventeen letters as thick casing cassia.

described: Fern of wet forest with fronds so thin they are almost transparent when held to the light, once divided into small oblong segments on a wiry black stalk, the spore lines running along the veins beneath.
traits: fronds thin enough to see light through; small oblong segments; wiry black stalk; spore lines along the veins; wet forest
name: film + fern
why: The thinness of the frond is what is seen the moment one is lifted, and it separates this from the leathery, lacy and fan-shaped ferns already named.

described: Minute leafy liverwort making a thin film on bark and living leaves, each leaf carrying a small pouch folded beneath it whose opening is bordered by a distinct thickened rim, like a lip around the mouth.
traits: thickened rim like a lip around the pouch mouth; minute; thin film on bark and living leaves; pouch folded under each leaf
name: lip + moss
why: It is a film moss like Lejeunea and differs at the rim of the pouch, which is what its name says in Greek and where the two are separated under a lens.

described: Of China. The country's own name for itself is 中国, the middle land, a land understood as lying at the centre of what its people knew.
traits: the middle land; China's own name read literally
name: middle + land
why: design.md says a place is answered by DESCRIBING it, and gives japonica as sun-begin-land. This is the same move on the name China uses for itself.

described: Of China, the middle land. The neuter of the same word.
traits: the middle land
name: middle + land
why: The neuter form of sinensis and the same place.

described: Of China, the middle land, 中国.
traits: the middle land
name: middle + land
why: A second spelling of the same place, which must read the same way or two names for one country enter the language.

described: Of China, the middle land, 中国.
traits: the middle land
name: middle + land
why: The neuter of chinensis.

described: Of Japan. 日本 is sun-origin: the land where the sun rises, named from the point of view of the mainland looking east.
traits: the land the sun rises from
name: sun + begin + land
why: This is design.md's own worked example for how a place is described rather than taken.

described: Of Japan, the land the sun rises from.
traits: the land the sun rises from
name: sun + begin + land
why: The neuter of japonica.

described: Of Japan, the land the sun rises from.
traits: the land the sun rises from
name: sun + begin + land
why: The masculine of japonica.

described: Of Taiwan. 台湾 is terrace-bay, for the stepped terraces above the western anchorage where the first settlements stood.
traits: terrace above a bay
name: terrace + bay
why: The island's Chinese name is a description of its own shore and reads literally.

described: Of Taiwan, the terrace above the bay.
traits: terrace above a bay
name: terrace + bay
why: A second form of the same place.

described: Of Taiwan under its older name, given by sailors who saw the forested mountains from the sea and called it the beautiful island.
traits: the beautiful island
name: beauty + island
why: Formosa is the Portuguese for beautiful, said of an island, and is a description rather than a name.

described: Of the beautiful island.
traits: the beautiful island
name: beauty + island
why: The masculine of formosana.

described: Of Yunnan. 云南 is cloud-south: the land south of the cloudy mountains, where the cloud sits on the ranges most of the year.
traits: south of the clouds
name: cloud + south
why: A Chinese province name that is a plain description of where it lies.

described: Of Yunnan, south of the clouds.
traits: south of the clouds
name: cloud + south
why: The neuter of yunnanensis.

described: Of Sichuan. 四川 is four-rivers, the basin drained by four great rivers running down to the Yangtze.
traits: the land of four rivers
name: four + river
why: The province is named for its rivers and the name says so.

described: Of Tibet. 西藏 is west-treasure, the western storehouse, seen from the Chinese side of the plateau.
traits: the western treasure house
name: west + hoard
why: The Chinese name for the region is a description of its position and its wealth.

described: Of Tibet, the western treasure house.
traits: the western treasure house
name: west + hoard
why: The neuter of tibetica.

described: Of the Himalaya. The Sanskrit is hima-alaya, the abode of snow, which is what the range is: the place snow lives.
traits: the dwelling of snow
name: snow + home
why: The range's own Sanskrit name is a description and needs no other.

described: Of the Himalaya, the dwelling of snow.
traits: the dwelling of snow
name: snow + home
why: A second form of the same range.

described: Of India. The name descends from Sindhu, the river, so the country is the river land, named by outsiders for the water they crossed to reach it.
traits: the land of the river
name: river + land
why: Every spelling of India traces back to a word meaning river, which is a description rather than a name.

described: Of India, the land of the river.
traits: the land of the river
name: river + land
why: The neuter of indica.

described: Of Mount Emei. 峨眉 is lofty-eyebrow, for the two high curved ridges that stand over the plain like a pair of painted brows.
traits: the high curved brow ridges
name: high + brow
why: The mountain's name is a picture of its own skyline, which is exactly what a described place should be.

described: Of Mount Emei, the high brow ridges.
traits: the high curved brow ridges
name: high + brow
why: An older spelling of emeiensis.

described: Of Guangxi. 广西 is broad-west, the western half of the old broad province.
traits: the broad west
name: broad + west
why: A Chinese province whose name states where it is.

described: Of Guangdong. 广东 is broad-east, the eastern half of the same old broad province.
traits: the broad east
name: broad + east
why: The pair to Guangxi and named the same way.

described: Of Hunan. 湖南 is lake-south, the land south of Dongting lake.
traits: south of the lake
name: lake + south
why: Named for its position against a lake, and the name says it.

described: Of Hubei. 湖北 is lake-north, the land north of the same lake.
traits: north of the lake
name: lake + north
why: The pair to Hunan.

described: Of Henan. 河南 is river-south, the land south of the Yellow River.
traits: south of the river
name: river + south
why: Named for its position against the river.

described: Of Hebei. 河北 is river-north, the land north of the Yellow River.
traits: north of the river
name: river + north
why: The pair to Henan.

described: Of Shandong. 山东 is mountain-east, the land east of the Taihang range.
traits: east of the mountains
name: mountain + east
why: Named for its position against a range.

described: Of Qinghai. 青海 is blue-sea, for the great salt lake on the plateau that gives the province its name.
traits: the blue sea lake
name: blue + sea
why: The lake is the province's name and the name is its colour.

described: Of Xinjiang. 新疆 is new-frontier, the territory added last to the empire's western edge.
traits: the new frontier
name: new + border
why: A name that states what the place was to whoever named it.

described: Of the Tian Shan. 天山 is heaven-mountain, a range high enough that its snow line stands against the sky.
traits: the mountains of the sky
name: sky + mountain
why: The range's name is a description of its height.

described: Of the Tian Shan, the mountains of the sky.
traits: the mountains of the sky
name: sky + mountain
why: A second spelling of the same range.

described: Of the Altai. The Mongolian altan is gold, so the range is the golden mountains, named for the metal taken out of them.
traits: the golden mountains
name: gold + mountain
why: The range's own name means gold and is a description of what it held.

described: Of Lake Baikal. The Turkic bay-kul is the rich lake, rich for the fish that fed everyone living around it.
traits: the rich lake
name: rich + lake
why: The lake's name describes what it gave, which survives a speaker who has never heard of it.

described: Of Muli, a high county in the mountains of south-west Sichuan, almost entirely under forest, deep valleys between ranges that hold snow most of the year.
traits: a high county under forest; deep valleys; snow on the ranges
name: high + forest + land
why: The Chinese 木里 is a sounding-out of a Tibetan name, so reading its characters would be reading a transliteration. The place itself is describable and this describes it.

described: Of Muli, the high forested county.
traits: a high county under forest
name: high + forest + land
why: The neuter of muliensis.

described: Of Hainan. 海南 is sea-south: the island lying south across the water from the mainland.
traits: the island south across the sea
name: sea + south
why: A Chinese place name that is a plain statement of where it lies.

described: Of Hainan, south across the sea.
traits: the island south across the sea
name: sea + south
why: The neuter of hainanensis.

described: Of Lushui, a county strung along a deep gorge of the Nu river in western Yunnan, the water running fast between walls of rock.
traits: a deep river gorge; fast water between rock walls
name: gorge + river
why: The county is the gorge it sits in, which is what anyone arriving there sees.

described: Of Luding, on the Dadu river in western Sichuan, known for the iron chain bridge slung across the gorge.
traits: a chain bridge over a river gorge; fast water
name: chain + bridge
why: The bridge is what the town is and what it is known for, and it is a thing rather than a name.

described: Of Wenchuan, a county in the mountains of Sichuan on the Min river, where the valley floor is narrow and the slopes rise steeply on both sides.
traits: a narrow river valley between steep slopes
name: narrow + valley
why: The Chinese 汶川 names a river and a plain, and the place is the valley it occupies.

described: Of Wenchuan, the narrow valley.
traits: a narrow river valley between steep slopes
name: narrow + valley
why: The neuter of wenchuanensis.

described: Of Jinggangshan. 井冈山 is well-ridge-mountain, a range of forested ridges with flat hollows between them that hold water like wells.
traits: forested ridges with water-holding hollows
name: well + ridge + mountain
why: The mountain's Chinese name describes its own shape and reads straight through.

described: Of Songpan, high grassland and pine country on the eastern edge of the Tibetan plateau, where the forest gives out into open pasture.
traits: high pine country; grassland at the forest edge
name: pine + high + land
why: The Chinese 松潘 opens with pine, and pine at altitude is what the place is.

described: Of Alishan, a high range in central Taiwan, cloud standing in the valleys below the summits most mornings, the slopes under old cypress forest.
traits: cloud standing in the valleys; high cypress forest; central Taiwan
name: cloud + forest + mountain
why: The Chinese is a sounding-out of an aboriginal name, so the place is described instead: cloud sea and cypress are what it is known and visited for.

described: Of Gaoligong, a long steep range running north to south on the Burmese border, so sharply ridged and so wet that the slopes carry different forest at every height.
traits: a long steep north-south ridge; wet slopes; forest changing with height; a border range
name: steep + border + range
why: The Chinese name sounds out a local one. The range's own shape, long and steep and on a border, is what can honestly be said of it.

described: Of Nyalam, a Tibetan town at the head of a gorge where the plateau breaks and falls away towards Nepal, the road running down through it.
traits: a gorge at the edge of the plateau; the way down to the lowland; a pass
name: gorge + pass
why: The name is Tibetan and the Chinese sounds it out, so the place is described: it is the pass where the plateau ends.

described: Of Luocheng, a county in the limestone hills of northern Guangxi, the ground broken into cones and caves.
traits: limestone hills broken into cones and caves; northern Guangxi
name: stone + cave + hill
why: The karst is what the county is made of and what is seen from any road in it.

described: Of Yangshuo, on the Li river in Guangxi, where the limestone rises out of flat paddy in isolated towers.
traits: limestone towers rising from flat paddy; a river winding between them
name: stone + tower
why: The towers are the place, and they are a shape rather than a name.

described: Of the Ussuri, a river running north through cold mixed forest along the eastern border, its valley holding both northern conifers and southern broadleaves.
traits: a northern river valley; mixed cold forest; an eastern border river
name: cold + forest + river
why: The river is named in a local language the Chinese sounds out, so what is described is the valley: a cold river running through mixed forest.

described: Of Kashgar, an oasis city on the western rim of the Taklamakan, watered by rivers off the mountains and ringed by desert beyond the irrigated land.
traits: an oasis ringed by desert; watered from the mountains; the western rim of a sand sea
name: oasis + sand + land
why: Kashgar is sounded out in Chinese and the name means nothing in it. The oasis in the desert is the place and is describable.

described: Of Kashgar, the oasis ringed by desert.
traits: an oasis ringed by desert
name: oasis + sand + land
why: The feminine of kaschgaricum.

described: Of the Pamirs, a high cold knot of ranges where several great mountain systems meet, bare above the tree line, grazed in summer and empty in winter.
traits: a high cold knot where ranges meet; bare above the tree line; summer grazing only
name: high + bare + range
why: The name is local and opaque in Chinese and in Latin both. What the place is, a bare high meeting of ranges, can be said plainly.

described: Of the Pamirs, the bare high ranges.
traits: a high cold knot where ranges meet; bare above the tree line
name: high + bare + range
why: The neuter of pamirica.

described: Of Lhasa. The Tibetan means place-of-the-gods, for the temple the city grew around, on a wide flat valley floor high on the plateau.
traits: the place of the gods; a wide high valley floor; a temple city
name: god + place
why: The Tibetan name is itself a description and reads straight through, which is the same move as japonica.

described: Of Tonkin, the north of Vietnam around the Red River delta. The name is 東京, eastern capital, the same two characters that make Tokyo.
traits: the eastern capital; a great river delta; the north of Vietnam
name: east + capital
why: The name is written in characters that say what it was, an eastern seat of government, and those read literally.

described: Of Dinghu. 鼎湖 is cauldron-lake, for the round steep-sided lake on the mountain that holds water like a pot.
traits: a round steep-sided lake like a cauldron; a forested mountain
name: cauldron + lake
why: The Chinese name is a picture of the lake's shape and needs nothing added.

described: Of Lijiang. 丽江 is beautiful-river, the old town on the upper Yangtze under the snow range, water running through every street.
traits: the beautiful river; water through every street; under a snow range
name: beauty + river
why: The name states what the place was named for and reads directly.

described: Of Guangxi, the broad west, under an older spelling.
traits: the broad west
name: broad + west
why: The same province as guangxiensis under the older romanisation, and it must read the same or one place gets two names.

described: Of Sichuan, the land of four rivers, under an older spelling.
traits: the land of four rivers
name: four + river
why: An older romanisation of sichuanensis and the same place.

described: Of Sichuan, the land of four rivers, under a German spelling.
traits: the land of four rivers
name: four + river
why: A third romanisation of the same province.

described: Of Guizhou. 贵州 is noble-region, a high limestone province of cones and gorges.
traits: the noble region; high limestone cones and gorges
name: noble + land
why: The Chinese name reads literally and the older spelling must reach the same reading as the modern one.

described: Of Fujian. 福建 is fortune-establish, the coastal province founded, as its name says, on good fortune.
traits: fortune established; a mountainous coast
name: luck + build
why: The name is two characters that both mean something and together say what was hoped of the place.

described: Of Henan, the land south of the Yellow River, under an older spelling.
traits: south of the river
name: river + south
why: An older romanisation of henanensis.

described: Of Hubei, the land north of the lake, under an older spelling.
traits: north of the lake
name: lake + north
why: An older romanisation of hubeiensis.

described: Of Jiangxi. 江西 is river-west, the land west of the Gan river's lower course.
traits: west of the river
name: river + west
why: A Chinese province named for its position against a river.

described: Of Liaoning. 辽宁 is distant-peace, the far north-eastern province, named for the quiet wanted on a frontier.
traits: distant peace; the far north-east
name: far + peace
why: Both characters carry sense and together they say what the place was meant to be.

described: Of the Qinling, the range running east to west across the middle of China that divides the wet south from the dry north, wooded on one flank and bare on the other.
traits: an east-west range dividing wet south from dry north; wooded one side, bare the other
name: divide + range
why: The range's name is a dynasty's, which says nothing. What it DOES, splitting the country's weather in two, is its defining fact.

described: Of Taibai Shan. 太白山 is great-white-mountain, the highest peak of the Qinling, snow on its head most of the year.
traits: the great white mountain; snow most of the year; highest of its range
name: great + white + mountain
why: The mountain's Chinese name describes its summit and reads straight through.

described: Of Moupin, a district on the eastern edge of the Tibetan mountains where the forest climbs from warm valley to snow line in a single day's walk.
traits: forest from warm valley to snow line; the eastern edge of the Tibetan mountains
name: steep + forest + edge
why: The name is a local one the Chinese sounds out, so the place is described by what makes it famous: the whole span of forest in one slope.

described: Of Siberia, the cold north: an unbroken belt of conifer forest over frozen ground, running further east than any other forest on earth.
traits: unbroken conifer forest; frozen ground; the far cold north
name: cold + north + forest
why: The name's origin is disputed and says nothing anyway. The forest on frozen ground is what the word means to anyone who uses it.

described: Of Siberia, the cold northern forest.
traits: unbroken conifer forest; frozen ground
name: cold + north + forest
why: The neuter of sibirica.

described: Of Dzungaria, a closed basin in the far north-west, sand and gravel steppe ringed by high ranges with no outlet to any sea.
traits: a closed basin with no outlet; sand and gravel steppe; ringed by high ranges
name: closed + basin
why: The name is Mongol and is sounded out in both Chinese and Latin. The basin itself, shut on every side, is the fact about it.

described: Of the Philippines, a scatter of thousands of islands in a warm sea, wet all year, each large island carrying its own plants.
traits: thousands of islands in a warm sea; wet all year; each island with its own plants
name: many + island + sea
why: The name is a Spanish king's and says nothing. The archipelago, many islands in warm water, is what the word points at.

described: Of Luzon, the largest of those islands, a long body of land with a spine of volcanoes down it.
traits: the largest island; a spine of volcanoes; warm and wet
name: big + island + fire + mountain
why: The name is local and opaque. What the island is, big and volcanic, can be said plainly.

described: Of the Amur. The Chinese name for the river is 黑龙江, black-dragon-river, for the dark water winding between forested banks in the far north-east.
traits: the black dragon river; dark winding water; forested northern banks
name: black + dragon + river
why: The river's Chinese name is a picture of it and reads straight through, which beats sounding out a Tungus name.

described: Of Dauria, the country east of Lake Baikal: cold open steppe running into larch forest, frozen hard for half the year.
traits: cold open steppe; larch forest; frozen half the year; east of a great lake
name: cold + steppe
why: The name is a people's and says nothing. The country is steppe that freezes, which is what the word points at.

described: Of Dauria, the cold steppe east of the great lake.
traits: cold open steppe; frozen half the year
name: cold + steppe
why: A second spelling of dahurica and the same country.

described: Of Korea. 高麗 is high-beautiful, the old kingdom's name for itself, a peninsula of steep wooded hills running down to the sea.
traits: the high and beautiful land; steep wooded hills; a peninsula
name: high + beauty + land
why: The kingdom's own name for itself is two characters that both carry sense, which is the japonica move again.

described: Of Korea, the high and beautiful land.
traits: the high and beautiful land; steep wooded hills
name: high + beauty + land
why: A second form of koraiensis.

described: Of Manchuria, the cold north-east: black soil plain ringed by wooded mountains, hot brief summers and long hard winters.
traits: black soil plain; wooded mountains around it; long hard winter, brief hot summer
name: black + soil + plain
why: The name is a people's. The place is a plain of famously black earth, which is a fact about the ground rather than about anyone.

described: Of Manchuria, the black soil plain.
traits: black soil plain; long hard winter
name: black + soil + plain
why: A second spelling of mandshurica.

described: Of Mongolia, a high dry plateau of short grass and gravel, too cold and too dry for trees over most of it, grazed and crossed rather than settled.
traits: a high dry plateau; short grass and gravel; too dry for trees; grazed and crossed
name: dry + grass + plateau
why: Mongol is a people, which the design refuses outright. The plateau itself, high and dry and treeless, is a fact about the ground.

described: Of Mongolia, the high dry plateau.
traits: a high dry plateau; short grass; too dry for trees
name: dry + grass + plateau
why: The masculine of mongolica.

described: Of Thailand. The country's own name says the land of the free, for never having been taken by an outside power, a warm wet land of river plains and monsoon forest.
traits: the free land; river plains and monsoon forest; warm and wet all year
name: free + land
why: The country's own name for itself carries a plain sense and is the better reading of the two available.

described: Of Annam. 安南 is peaceful-south, the old name for the long coastal country south of China, mountains on one side and sea on the other.
traits: the peaceful south; a long coast; mountains inland of it
name: peace + south
why: Two characters that both mean something, naming the place by where it sat and what was wanted of it.

described: Of Okinawa. 沖縄 is offshore-rope, for the chain of small islands strung out in the open sea south of the main Japanese lands.
traits: a rope of islands strung offshore; warm open sea; small islands in a chain
name: offshore + rope
why: The Japanese name is a picture of the island chain seen on a map or from a boat.

described: Of Kyushu. 九州 is nine-provinces, the southern island of Japan, warm and volcanic, once divided into nine.
traits: the nine provinces; a warm volcanic island; southern Japan
name: nine + land
why: A place named by counting what it was made of, which reads directly.

described: Of Beijing. 北京 is north-capital, the seat of government in the north of the country.
traits: the northern capital; a seat of government
name: north + capital
why: The city's name states exactly what it is, and Tonkin and Nanjing are named the same way.

described: Of Nanjing. 南京 is south-capital, the southern seat, on the lower Yangtze.
traits: the southern capital; on a great river
name: south + capital
why: The pair to Beijing, named by the same rule.

described: Of Shanghai. 上海 is upon-the-sea, the city built where the river meets the coast, on flat ground barely above the water.
traits: upon the sea; where a great river meets the coast; flat ground barely above water
name: on + sea
why: The name says where the place sits and nothing else, which is what a described place should do.

described: Of Ningxia. 宁夏 is peaceful-summer, dry loess country along the upper Yellow River where irrigation makes a green strip through desert.
traits: peaceful summer; a green irrigated strip through desert; the upper Yellow River
name: peace + summer
why: Both characters carry sense and together name what was hoped of a hard country.

described: Of Dali. 大理 is great-order, an old kingdom on a lake under a long snow range in western Yunnan.
traits: the great order; a lake under a long snow range; western Yunnan
name: great + order
why: The old kingdom's name is two characters that both mean something.

described: Of Gansu, a long narrow corridor between desert and mountain, the road west running through it with oasis towns strung along the way.
traits: a long narrow corridor; desert one side, mountain the other; oasis towns along a road
name: narrow + corridor
why: The province is a passage rather than a region, and that shape is its defining fact.

described: Of Shanxi. 山西 is mountain-west, the loess plateau west of the Taihang range.
traits: west of the mountains; loess plateau
name: mountain + west
why: Named for its position against a range, like Shandong to its east.

described: Of Zhejiang. 浙江 is the crooked river, for the Qiantang's sharp bends before it reaches the sea.
traits: the crooked river; sharp bends before the sea; a coastal province
name: crooked + river
why: The province takes its name from the river's shape, which is a description.

described: Of Anhui, the country either side of the lower Huai and Yangtze, flat and wet in the north, hilly and wooded in the south.
traits: flat wet plain in the north, wooded hills in the south; two great rivers
name: two + river + land
why: The name is made from two city names and says nothing. The province is the land between two rivers, which does.

described: Of Qionglai, a range on the western rim of the Sichuan basin where the land steps up abruptly from plain to high mountain.
traits: the land steps abruptly from plain to mountain; the western rim of a basin
name: step + range
why: The name sounds out a local one. The abrupt step from plain to mountain is what the range is.

described: Of Kashmir, a broad flat valley floor held between two mountain walls, lakes on the floor of it and meadow above the treeline on both sides.
traits: a flat valley floor between two mountain walls; lakes on the floor; meadow above the trees
name: held + valley
why: Kashmir is distinct from Kashgar, which the corpus confuses. The shut valley between ranges is what the place is and what everyone who describes it describes.

described: Of Kashmir, the valley held between mountain walls.
traits: a flat valley floor between two mountain walls
name: held + valley
why: The neuter of kashmirensis.

described: Of Kashmir, the held valley.
traits: a flat valley floor between two mountain walls
name: held + valley
why: An older spelling of the same valley.

described: Of Aba, a high Tibetan region of north-west Sichuan: open grassland at great height with wide peat marshes lying in the hollows, treeless and cold.
traits: high open grassland; wide peat marsh in the hollows; treeless and cold
name: high + marsh + grass
why: The name is Tibetan and the Chinese sounds it out. The high marsh grassland is unmistakable and is what the region is.

described: Of Ngari, the far west of Tibet: the highest, driest and emptiest part of the plateau, bare rock and salt lakes with almost nothing growing between them.
traits: the highest and driest plateau; bare rock and salt lakes; almost nothing grows
name: bare + high + waste
why: The Chinese 阿里 sounds out a Tibetan name. What the place is, the emptiest high ground there is, can be said without it.

described: Of Gongshan, in the gorges where three great rivers run parallel a few days' walk apart, the ridges between them so steep that the forest changes completely from river to summit.
traits: three great rivers running parallel; ridges so steep the forest changes with height; deep gorges
name: three + river + gorge
why: The place is famous for exactly one thing, the parallel gorges, and that is a fact about the ground rather than a name.

described: Of western Hunan, a country of limestone gorges and caves with rivers running underground and reappearing, the hills steep and close together.
traits: limestone gorges and caves; rivers running underground; steep close hills
name: cave + gorge + land
why: 湘西 is west-Hunan, an abbreviation rather than a description, so the karst that the region is made of does the work.

described: Of Leye, where the limestone has collapsed into enormous round sinkholes hundreds of paces across, each holding its own patch of forest at the bottom.
traits: enormous round collapsed sinkholes; forest growing at the bottom of each; limestone
name: sink + hole
why: The sinkholes are what the county is known for and are visible from the air, which is as obvious as a place gets.

described: Of Lichuan, a valley in the Hubei mountains where the dawn redwood was found still living after being known only from stone.
traits: the valley where a tree thought lost was found alive; mountain valley in Hubei
name: lost + tree + valley
why: The find is what the place means to anyone who has heard of it, and it is an event rather than a person.

described: Of Ruili, on the Burmese border where the plateau drops into hot lowland, monsoon forest and banana country right up against the hills.
traits: where the plateau drops to hot lowland; monsoon forest; a border town
name: hot + border + low
why: The name is Dai and is sounded out in Chinese. The drop from cool plateau to hot lowland is the place.

described: Of Ruoqiang, on the southern rim of the Lop desert: salt crust, dry riverbeds and wind-cut ground, one of the emptiest places anywhere.
traits: salt crust and dry riverbeds; wind-cut ground; the rim of a desert; almost empty
name: salt + waste
why: The name sounds out a local one. The salt desert is the whole of what is there.

described: Of Burqin, in the foothills of the Altai where birch and larch forest runs down to a clear river out of the gold mountains.
traits: birch and larch forest; a clear river out of the mountains; Altai foothills
name: birch + river
why: The Chinese sounds out a Mongol name. The birch forest along the river is what the place looks like.

described: Of Sayram, a cold blue lake held high in the Tianshan with no river running out of it, grassland running down to the shore.
traits: a cold blue lake held high in the mountains; no outlet; grassland to the shore
name: high + blue + lake
why: The lake is the place and its colour and height are what everyone remarks on.

described: Of Eluanbi, the southernmost cape of Taiwan: raised coral limestone standing over the sea, wind-bent scrub on top of it.
traits: the southernmost cape; raised coral limestone; wind-bent scrub over the sea
name: south + cape
why: A cape at the end of an island is a shape rather than a name, and this one is the end of it.

described: Of Wuyuan, a country of terraced hills in Jiangxi, old villages under camphor trees with the fields cut in steps up every slope.
traits: terraced hills; fields cut in steps; old villages under great camphor trees
name: step + field + hill
why: The terracing is what the place is famous for and is the shape of the whole landscape.

described: Of Langao, in the Daba mountains where the range rises in mist off the Han river, wet forest on the northern slopes.
traits: mist rising off a river into mountains; wet forest on north slopes; the Daba range
name: mist + mountain
why: The Chinese 岚 is the mist that rises in a mountain valley, which is both the name's own sense and the place.

described: Of Malipo, limestone hills on the Vietnamese border, wet and warm, the rock broken into ridges holding forest in every crack.
traits: limestone ridges on a border; wet and warm; forest in every crack of the rock
name: border + stone + hill
why: The corpus reads the Latin as bad-exist, which is two guesses. The karst border country is the place.

described: Of the Tumen, the river marking the Korean border, cold and shallow, running through low wooded hills to a short stretch of sea.
traits: a cold shallow border river; low wooded hills; a short run to the sea
name: border + river
why: The river is named in Manchu and sounded out. It is a border and a river, which is all anyone needs.

described: Of Yuelu, a wooded hill standing over the river at Changsha with an old academy on its slope, maples turning the whole hill red in autumn.
traits: a wooded hill over a river; maples reddening the whole hill in autumn; an old school on its slope
name: maple + hill
why: The autumn colour is what the hill is visited for and is a fact about what grows there.

described: Of Lhorong, in eastern Tibet where the plateau is cut into deep dry valleys, grazing on the high ground and barley on the valley floors.
traits: deep dry valleys cut into a plateau; grazing above, barley below
name: dry + valley + high
why: The Chinese sounds out a Tibetan name. The dry cut valleys are the shape of the country.

described: From beyond Alishan, the far side of the cloud and cypress range in central Taiwan.
traits: the far side of the cloud forest range
name: across + cloud + mountain
why: Built on arisanensis, which is already described, with the crossing said plainly.

described: Of Borneo, a great equatorial island under unbroken rain forest, rivers running brown with peat out of swamp forest behind the coast.
traits: a great equatorial island; unbroken rain forest; brown peat rivers; swamp behind the coast
name: rain + forest + island
why: The name is local and opaque. The island is forest and rain on a scale that is the fact about it.

described: Of Suriname, a low tropical coast of mud and mangrove backed by unbroken forest on old hard rock, the rivers running north to the sea.
traits: a low muddy tropical coast; mangrove; unbroken forest inland; rivers running north
name: mud + coast + forest
why: The corpus reads it as super-town-month, three guesses. The coast and the forest behind it are the country.

described: Legume shrub with small pinnate leaves and yellow or coppery pea flowers, whose pods blow up into thin papery bladders that stay closed and pop loudly when squeezed.
traits: pods inflated into papery bladders; pop when squeezed; yellow or coppery pea flower; small pinnate leaf
name: bladder + pod
why: Chinese yu biao huai is fish-bladder locust, naming the same inflated pod. Bursting one is what anyone does on meeting the shrub.

described: Low herb whose rounded leaf is folded into pleats like a fan and edged with fine teeth, and whose surface throws water off so completely that dew stands on it in whole round beads until the sun is high.
traits: dew standing in whole round beads on the leaf; leaf folded in pleats like a fan; fine-toothed edge
name: dew + leaf
why: The beaded dew is the one thing everyone who meets the plant remembers, and it is a property of the leaf surface rather than a story about it.

described: Tree whose fruit is dry and hardly worth eating, while the STALKS that carry it swell, redden and turn sweet and fleshy as they ripen, tasting of raisins, and those are what is picked.
traits: the fruit stalks swell and sweeten, not the fruit; taste of raisins; dry inedible fruit above them
name: sweet + stalk
why: A tree where the stalk is the food and the fruit is not is unusual enough to name by, and it is what the tree is grown for.

described: Climbing gourd whose round brown fruit, dried hard, is so intensely sweet that a fragment of it sweetens a whole pot, and it is simmered for coughs and sore throats.
traits: a small round brown gourd; intensely sweet dried; simmered for cough; a climbing vine
name: sweet + gourd
why: Chinese luo han guo names it for a monk, which says nothing about it. The sweetness is extreme, is the whole use, and is a fact about the fruit.

described: Grey softly felted leaves and upright spikes of four-petalled flowers, purple, white or cream, which give almost no scent by day and pour it out after dark strongly enough to fill a garden.
traits: scent released after dark, not by day; grey felted leaf; upright spike of four-petalled flowers
name: night + scent
why: Scenting only at night is what the plant is grown for and is unmistakable, since the same flower is nearly odourless at noon.

described: Small weak-stemmed herb of shade and rock crevice with narrow opposite leaves and tiny white flowers, whose black seed carries a pale fleshy knob that ants take hold of and carry away.
traits: seed with a pale fleshy knob; ants carry the seeds off by it; small white flower; shaded rock crevice
name: seed + knob
why: Chinese zhong fu cao is seed-mound grass, naming the same knob. It is why the plant turns up in ant country and nowhere else.

described: Shrub whose flowers open deep purple, fade through pale lavender the next day and are white by the third, so that all three colours stand on the bush at once.
traits: flowers open purple, fade lavender, then white; all three colours at once on one bush; scented
name: fade + flower
why: The fading is the plant: three colours on one shrub on any given morning, which is why English calls it yesterday-today-tomorrow.

described: Coarse grass of wet ground whose seed sits inside a hard shining case, grey or white, round and pierced through, hard enough to thread on a string and worn as beads as well as boiled and eaten.
traits: hard shining seed case, pierced through; strung as beads; also boiled and eaten; wet ground
name: bead + grass
why: The seed is literally used as a bead and has been for thousands of years, which is both a use and an exact description of its shape.

described: Woodland herb whose leathery leaf is cut into three rounded lobes and turns a dark liver colour through winter, holding on under the snow while the early blue flowers come up beside it.
traits: leaf in three rounded lobes; turns dark liver colour in winter; holds through snow; early blue flower
name: liver + leaf
why: The lobed leaf and its winter colour are both in the name in Latin and in English, and the resemblance is plain when the leaf is turned over.

described: Mallow standing head high or taller on a single unbranched stem, hung along its whole length with wide flat open flowers the width of a palm, rough hairy heart-shaped leaves below.
traits: head high or taller on one unbranched stem; wide flat flowers the width of a palm; rough hairy leaf
name: tall + mallow
why: Its height on a single stem is what picks it out of a garden from across a street, and it is a mallow, which places it exactly.

described: Herb whose flower head is packed so densely and flattened so far that it curls into a ridged crest like the comb of a cockerel, in hot red, orange or yellow, dry to the touch.
traits: flower head flattened into a ridged crest like a cockerel's comb; hot dry colours; stiff and papery
name: comb + flower
why: The crested head is unlike any other flower shape and is what the plant is grown for. English and Chinese both reach for the same comparison.

described: Grey aromatic sub-shrub of dry stony ground with narrow leaves and short spikes of small blue flowers, cut and dried and laid among stored clothes to keep the moth out and leave its scent behind.
traits: laid among stored clothes; strong scent held after drying; grey narrow leaf; dry stony ground; short blue spike
name: cloth + scent
why: Chinese xun yi cao is scent-clothes grass, which names the use exactly: the plant is dried and put with linen, and has been for centuries.

described: Slight umbellifer of hedge and field edge with finely cut leaves and small white umbels, whose ripe fruits are covered in hooked bristles and come away on anything brushing past.
traits: fruits covered in hooked bristles; come away on clothing and fur; finely cut leaf; small white umbel; hedge and field edge
name: cling + seed
why: Chinese qie yi is steal-clothes, which is exactly what it does. The plant is usually discovered on the walk home rather than in the field.

described: Slender twining vine of warm forest with opposite leaves and loose hanging sprays of small flowers on thread-fine stalks, the whole spray swinging clear of the foliage like a hung curtain.
traits: flower sprays hanging clear on thread-fine stalks; slender twiner; warm forest; opposite leaves
name: curtain + vine
why: Chinese lian zi teng is curtain vine, for the way the flower sprays hang free of the leaves and move together.

described: Low spreading legume whose leaf is a single pair of leaflets set opposite each other at the top of the stalk, like two blades of a scissors, with small yellow pea flowers in a bracted spike.
traits: leaf of exactly one opposite pair of leaflets; low and spreading; small yellow pea flower in a bracted spike
name: pair + leaf
why: A leaf of exactly two leaflets is countable at a glance and separates it from every trifoliate legume around it.

described: Poppy of dry open ground and cornfield in the far west, with finely cut leaves and violet or deep red flowers whose petals crumple and drop within a day, over a long narrow seed pod.
traits: violet or deep red poppy; petals crumple and drop within a day; long narrow pod; dry open ground
name: field + poppy
why: Chinese jiang ying su is frontier poppy. It is a poppy of open cultivated and waste ground, which is what field says.

described: Moss of bog pool and wet hollow, often flushed deep red or purple, its shoots soft and loosely branched and frequently under water for part of the year.
traits: grows in bog pools and wet hollows; often deep red or purple; soft loosely branched shoots; often submerged
name: pool + moss
why: The Chinese names a person. Living in standing water separates it from the peat moss that builds the bog around it and from the dry-ground mosses.

described: Very small moss making close thin dark mats on rock and tree base, finer even than the thin moss it is named against, the shoots thread-like and closely leaved.
traits: finer and thinner than Leskea; thread-like closely leaved shoots; close dark mats on rock and tree base
name: fine + moss
why: Chinese xi luo xian is fine-gauze moss and fine is exactly the difference from the thin moss beside it.

described: Moss hanging from bark in warm wet forest, the shoots flattened and the leaves broad and blunt with a rounded tip, so a shoot reads as a row of small spoons.
traits: shoots flattened, leaves broad and blunt with rounded tips; hangs from bark; warm wet forest
name: spoon + moss
why: Chinese piao ye xian is gourd-leaf moss, reaching for the same rounded blade. The blunt broad leaf is what separates it under a lens.

described: Low spiny legume of salt desert and dry steppe, its branches ending in stiff green thorns, small red pea flowers among them. Camels eat it where there is nothing else, and in heat it sweats a sugar that dries on the twigs and is gathered.
traits: stiff green thorns at every branch end; salt desert and dry steppe; eaten by camels; sweats a gatherable sugar
name: camel + thorn
why: Chinese luo tuo ci is camel thorn and so is the English. Two traditions that never met named it for the same two facts.

described: Great woody liana of wet tropical forest hanging long chains of claw-shaped flowers whose colour is a luminous blue-green found almost nowhere else in a flower, each bloom curved like a talon.
traits: hanging chains of claw-shaped flowers; luminous blue-green colour; great woody liana; wet tropical forest
name: jade + vine
why: Chinese fei cui ge is jade vine and jade is exactly the colour, which is the whole reason anyone knows the plant.

described: Great bulb throwing up a thick hollow stalk with no leaves on it, carrying two to six enormous flaring trumpets, scarlet or white or striped, the strap leaves following afterwards.
traits: enormous flaring trumpet flowers; thick hollow leafless stalk; a great bulb; leaves come after the flowers
name: trumpet + bulb
why: The flower's shape and the bulb it comes out of are both unmistakable, and the flower arriving before the leaves is the thing people remark on.

described: Tall laurel of warm forest whose timber is straight, fine-grained, faintly fragrant and a soft gold in colour, so durable it was reserved for the pillars and beams of palaces and coffins.
traits: straight fine golden timber; faintly fragrant wood; very durable; reserved for palace pillars
name: pillar + wood
why: Chinese nan mu names the timber, and that timber, cut for columns because it stands straight and lasts, is what the tree is to anyone who uses it.

described: Conifer whose flat sprays of scale leaves are marked underneath with broad chalk-white bands so bold that a branch turned over looks painted.
traits: broad chalk-white bands under flat leaf sprays; a branch turned over looks painted; flat scale-leaf sprays
name: white + back
why: The white underside is visible from the ground and from a distance and is what separates it from every other scale-leaved conifer.

described: Moss hanging in flattened glossy sprays from bark and shaded rock, the shoots pressed flat so that a spray lies in one plane like a pinned frond.
traits: flattened glossy sprays lying in one plane; hangs from bark and shaded rock; shoots pressed flat
name: flat + shine + moss
why: The Chinese names a person. Lying flat in a single plane and catching light is what the moss looks like and is how it is picked out.

described: Water plant rooted in mud with long strap leaves floating flat on the surface, sending up a stalk that clears the water and then FORKS into two spikes of small scented flowers.
traits: flower stalk forks into two spikes above the water; long strap leaves floating flat; rooted in mud
name: fork + water + herb
why: The forked spike standing clear of the water is the character of the genus and is visible from the bank.

described: Slender cane bamboo of thicket and streamside, running at the root into dense stands, the canes straight and thin and of a size to cut for fencing and baskets.
traits: slender straight canes in dense running stands; cut for fencing and baskets; streamside thicket
name: fence + bamboo
why: Chinese qing li zhu is green-fence bamboo, naming the use. It separates this from the thorn, arrow, wrapping and high bamboos already named.

described: Grass of marsh edge and wet field whose spikelets are flattened round and packed in two neat rows along one side of each branch, so the head reads as a row of small coins.
traits: flattened round spikelets packed in two rows on one side; marsh edge and wet field; head like a row of coins
name: coin + marsh + grass
why: The flattened spikelets set in two ranks are unlike the open or spike-like heads of the other wet-ground grasses already named.

described: Small moss whose leaves are turned sharply upward and back against the stem so that a shoot looks combed the wrong way, growing in low tufts on soil and rock.
traits: leaves turned sharply up and back against the stem; a shoot looks combed backwards; low tufts
name: up + leaf + moss
why: Chinese yang ye xian is upturned-leaf moss, naming the one thing that separates it under a lens.

described: Low grey much-branched shrublet of cold desert and stony steppe in the far west, the whole plant aromatic, with small tight heads of dull flowers and leaves cut into narrow grey segments.
traits: low grey aromatic shrublet; cold desert and stony steppe; narrow grey cut leaves; small tight flower heads
name: desert + daisy
why: It is a daisy that has become a desert shrub, which is what separates it from the herbs of its family, and the Chinese names it for Kashgar, a place rather than a trait.

described: Woody climber of the grape kin with palmate leaves of five leaflets and forked tendrils opposite them, carrying small dark berries in loose bunches, the bark peeling in strips.
traits: grape kin with forked tendrils; palmate leaves of five leaflets; small dark berries in loose bunches; peeling bark
name: wild + grape
why: It is a grape in everything but the fruit's size and sweetness, so naming it the wild one places it exactly against the vine everyone knows.

described: Small ginger of forest shade whose flower spike arches over and hangs, the yellow or orange flowers held far out on long slender curved stalks so that they shake and turn at the least movement of air while the rest of the plant stands still.
traits: flowers on long slender curved stalks that shake in any air; arching hanging spike; yellow or orange; small forest ginger
name: shake + ginger
why: Chinese wu hua jiang is dancing-flower ginger. Dance has no root and would not earn one on eleven species, and shake is already seated and says the same motion, so the name costs nothing and reads at once.

described: Of Changbai. 长白山 is ever-white-mountain, a volcano on the Korean border whose bare pale summit and crater lake hold snow far into the summer.
traits: ever white summit; a crater lake; a volcano on a border; snow late into summer
name: long + white + mountain
why: The mountain's Chinese name states the one thing visible from any distance, which is that its head is white all year.

described: Of the Hengduan. 横断山 is transverse-cut mountains, the ranges that run north to south and cut ACROSS the general east-west grain of the country, so that every valley is a wall between two others.
traits: ranges running across the grain of the country; every valley walled from the next; north-south ridges
name: cross + cut + range
